item.title: BNP’s 48th founding anniversary Tuesday
item.description:
The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) is observing its 48th founding anniversary on Tuesday, with a series of programs in Dhaka and across the country.
The party was founded by then president Ziaur Rahman on September 1, 1978, and has since remained one of Bangladesh’s major political forces, alternating between periods in government and opposition.
Marking the occasion, BNP Chairman and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman extended greetings to party leaders and activists, supporters, well-wishers and the people of Bangladesh.
In a message, Tarique described the anniversary as a day of “joy, enthusiasm and inspiration” and said the BNP’s history was marked by “courage, struggle, sacrifice and success.”
He said Ziaur Rahman founded the BNP in September 1978 at the premises of Ramna Restaurant in Dhaka, describing the move as a landmark in the country’s political history and the restoration of democracy.
Tarique said the one-party system, Baksal, was introduced on January 25, 1975, curtailing freedom of speech, individual liberty and democracy. He claimed Ziaur Rahman later restored democracy and reinstated the right of banned political parties to engage in politics.
Against this backdrop, Tarique said, the BNP was founded in response to the political needs of the time and contributed to the revival of multiparty democracy.
He paid tribute to Ziaur Rahman, describing him as the founder of the BNP and a statesman who played a role in shaping modern Bangladesh.
He also paid tribute to former prime minister and BNP chairperson Khaleda Zia, saying her leadership helped expand the party’s support base across the country.
Tarique said the BNP had worked to protect the country’s independence and sovereignty while pursuing democracy and good governance.
He also recalled the contributions of party leaders and activists who were killed or injured during movements for democracy and good governance.
According to Tarique, the BNP was entrusted with governing the country whenever people had the opportunity to vote freely in fair and credible elections.
He said the party undertook various initiatives while in power to strengthen and institutionalize democracy, including the restoration of parliamentary democracy and expansion of women’s education.
Tarique said that after what he described as more than a decade of “fascist rule and exploitation,” the people again entrusted the BNP with governing the country through a free, fair and neutral election.
“The BNP wants to repay the people’s trust by establishing an accountable state,” he said, adding that his government was working to build Bangladesh as a welfare-oriented state.
He urged party leaders, activists, supporters and well-wishers to remain committed to serving the country and preserving public trust.
Tarique said the people of Bangladesh, particularly those committed to democracy, were the source of the BNP’s political strength. He described the party as synonymous with the struggle to build a welfare-oriented, democratic and self-reliant Bangladesh.
The BNP has announced a five-day program to mark its founding anniversary.
The program was announced at a press conference at the party’s Nayapaltan central office last Wednesday by BNP Secretary General and the prime minister’s political adviser Ruhul Kabir Rizvi.
Party flags will be hoisted at 6am today at the central office and party offices across the country.
At 9am, Tarique Rahman, the acting secretary general, central leaders, and leaders and activists of the party’s affiliated and associate organizations will pay floral tributes and offer prayers at the graves of Ziaur Rahman and Khaleda Zia.
A discussion titled “The Purpose and Significance of the Establishment of the BNP” will be held at the Krishibid Institution Bangladesh auditorium at 3pm on September 5.
Tarique Rahman will attend the program as the chief guest, while senior BNP leaders and prominent intellectuals are expected to participate.
The party will also publish posters and organize tree-planting and fish-release programs.
BNP Joint Secretary General Habib-un-Nabi Khan Sohel will lead the fish-release program, while Joint Secretary General and Water Resources Minister Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee will lead the tree-planting program.
District and metropolitan BNP units, along with other grassroots units, will organize discussions and other programs across the country.
The BNP was established on September 1, 1978, with nationalism, independence, sovereignty and multiparty democracy becoming key elements of its political philosophy.
Ziaur Rahman, the party’s founding chairman, was assassinated on May 30, 1981. His wife, Khaleda Zia, subsequently took over the party’s leadership.
Under her leadership, the BNP came to power three times, with Khaleda Zia serving as prime minister during each term.
Over nearly five decades, the BNP has alternated between government and opposition while leading and participating in various political movements.
The party is marking its 48th anniversary with programs being organized by its central leadership as well as grassroots units across the country.

item.title: MSF: Killings, political violence, minority attacks rise in August
item.description:
Killings, political violence and attacks on minority communities increased in August compared to the previous month, while incidents of violence against women and children also rose, according to the Manabadhikar Shongskriti Foundation (MSF).
The number of people killed in incidents involving women and children jumped nearly 75%, while injuries in political violence surged 181%, the rights organization said in its monthly review of the country’s human rights situation released yesterday.
According to the report, 91 women and children were killed in August, compared to 52 in July.
Violence against women and children also increased from 306 incidents in July to 327 in August, marking a 6.8% rise.
Gang rape cases increased by 72%, while rape and murder cases increased by 67%. Suicide rose by 39%, abduction and disappearance by 8%, and illegal village arbitration by 33%. The number of people detained in drug-related cases increased by 129%.
MSF expressed particular concern over the sharp rise in political violence in August.
The number of people injured in political violence increased from 95 in July to 267 in August, an increase of 181%. Deaths, however, declined from seven to five.
The incidents involved activists and supporters of the BNP, National Citizens Party (NCP), Jamaat-e-Islami and Awami League, as well as internal and inter-party conflicts, according to the report.
MSF said ensuring the safety of political activists and ordinary citizens and creating an environment conducive to peaceful political activities were increasingly important for restoring democratic governance.
In cases filed following the 2024 anti-discrimination student movement and the fall of the government, the number of accused declined from 600 in July to 240 in August. Arrests in those cases, however, increased from 126 to 205.
Meanwhile, arrests during special drives increased from 5,196 in July to 5,618 in August, with a large proportion linked to drug-related cases.
Violence against minority communities also increased sharply in August.
MSF documented 26 incidents involving minorities during the month, compared to eight in July.
The incidents included vandalism of religious idols in Faridpur and Chittagong, attacks on members of minority communities, deaths and threats.
The report also highlighted the gang rape of a teenage girl in Lalmai, Cumilla, and the recovery of the body of a Tripura woman in Khagrachhari. The woman’s family alleged that she had been raped and murdered and called for a proper investigation.
MSF said the incidents underscored the need for stronger state and social initiatives to protect minorities, ensure equal rights and religious freedom, and preserve social harmony.
The recovery of unidentified bodies was another major concern in August.
A total of 71 unidentified bodies were recovered during the month, compared to 56 in July.
Of them, 55 were men and 14 were women, while the sex and age of two bodies could not be determined.
Most of the bodies were recovered from rivers, ponds, roads, railway tracks, under bridges, crop fields and abandoned locations. Some were reportedly found with their throats slit, inside sacks, with their hands and feet tied, or covered in blood.
MSF called for proper identification, autopsies, determination of causes of death, investigation and timely handover of the bodies to their families.
However, it cautioned that unidentified bodies should not automatically be equated with murder, enforced disappearance or extrajudicial killing without proper investigation.
Deaths in law enforcement custody declined from two in July to one in August, while deaths in prison custody fell from nine to five.
MSF said the decline was positive in numerical terms but should not be considered evidence of a long-term improvement.
Attacks on journalists increased slightly from 36 in July to 37 in August. Most journalists were attacked while collecting news. One journalist was arrested and another faced a case, according to the report.
Cyber-related cases and arrests declined, although MSF stressed the need to maintain a balance between law enforcement and freedom of expression.
Border-related rights concerns continued, including shootings of Bangladeshi citizens, allegations of torture by the Border Security Force (BSF), arrests, landmine explosions along the Myanmar border and attempts to push Bangladeshi citizens into the country.
Push-in attempts from the Indian border, however, fell from 100 in July to 15 in August.
MSF said the overall human rights situation remained concerning despite declines in some areas.
It called for stronger rule of law, prevention of mob justice and political violence, safeguards against arbitrary arrests, accountability in custody and prisons, protection of journalists and freedom of expression, and greater security for minorities and marginalized communities.
The organization also urged prompt, impartial and effective investigations into serious human rights violations, including cases involving unidentified bodies, and called for those responsible to be held accountable.

item.title: 424 outlets discharge 330 tons of waste into Dhaka rivers daily
item.description:
More than 424 government and private discharge points release around 330,000kg of liquid and solid waste into the Buriganga, Turag, Balu and Shitalakkhya rivers around Dhaka every day, with industries accounting for nearly 60% of the pollution, according to a Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Authority (BIWTA) survey.
The survey identified untreated industrial effluent, sewage, household waste, plastic, oil, burnt lubricants and other solid waste as major pollutants. Of the 424 identified discharge points, 244 are linked to privately owned factories and industrial establishments.
Another 30% of the pollution enters the rivers through drainage systems operated by city corporations, Dhaka Water Supply and Sewerage Authority (WASA) and local government bodies, while household and other sources account for the remaining 10%.
The findings come as the government has renewed efforts to tackle pollution in the rivers surrounding Dhaka following a series of meetings, a research report and field inspections in recent months.
A BIWTA action plan says nearly 7,000 small and large industrial establishments operate along the rivers around Dhaka, with around 99% reportedly lacking effluent treatment plants (ETPs).
Industrial establishments account for around 60% of the pollution, the action plan says. Other major sources include brick kilns, polythene, dockyards, burnt engine oil, vessels and household waste.
Experts say chemical industries and tanneries pose particularly serious risks because their wastewater can contain toxic chemicals.
The survey found 66 WASA drains directly connected to the Buriganga and Turag. Of these, 57 discharge into the Buriganga and nine into the Turag.
Dhaka South City Corporation has 21 identified drains, including 19 connected to the Buriganga and two to the Shitalakkhya. Dhaka North City Corporation has 16, with one connected to the Buriganga and 15 to the Turag.
Narayanganj City Corporation has 37 drains discharging into the Shitalakkhya, while four Gazipur City Corporation drains discharge into the Turag. Two drains from Postogola Cantonment are connected to the Buriganga.
Local government bodies also contribute to the pollution. Three Kutubpur Union Parishad drains, one from Zinjira, two from Kalindi and two from Shakta are connected to the Buriganga, while three Kaundia Union Parishad drains discharge into the Turag.
The Shitalakkhya receives waste through 10 drains from Rupganj Municipality, five from Tabaro Municipality, one from Kanchan Municipality, one from Ghorashal Municipality, and two from Baligaon and Kaliganj municipalities. Two Kanchpur Union Parishad drains and another Rupganj Municipality drain also discharge into the river.
A Bangladesh Water Development Board drain has also been identified as a pollution source in the Turag.
The Buriganga remains one of the starkest examples of Dhaka's environmental degradation. Its water has lost its natural color in many stretches, while dissolved oxygen levels have at times approached zero. Around 5mg per liter is generally considered necessary to sustain fish and other aquatic organisms.
Studies have also detected antibiotic residues in Buriganga water, including amoxicillin, penicillin, ciprofloxacin and azithromycin. Experts warn that pharmaceutical residues could contribute to antimicrobial resistance, particularly when untreated hospital and healthcare waste enters drainage systems.
Black oil, burnt lubricants and other petroleum-based waste from vessels are also regularly released into the rivers. Markets and riverside settlements contribute rotten vegetables, fruit, polythene, plastic and food waste to the waterways.
The rivers have remained severely polluted despite years of dredging, beautification, eviction drives and other restoration initiatives.
The latest government push followed a series of meetings and decisions beginning in July.
A July 1 meeting between the prime minister and city corporation authorities discussed issues related to the Dhaka Inner Circular Road and broader urban development. The discussions were followed by renewed attention to the deteriorating condition of the capital's surrounding rivers.
A meeting on August 2 discussed measures to improve the water quality and environmental condition of the Buriganga, Turag and other rivers around Dhaka.
A research report published on August 4 identified pollution sources and outlined recommendations to address the problem. The report was subsequently circulated to relevant ministries, departments and agencies for necessary action.
A follow-up meeting was held on August 6 to discuss the findings and determine the responsibilities of the relevant agencies.
On August 26, committee members held another meeting and conducted a field visit to assess the condition of the rivers. The delegation included the Planning Adviser, Shipping Adviser, Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister, secretaries of various ministries and senior officials of relevant government agencies.
The committee is scheduled to meet again on September 1 at the Office of the Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister to review the latest situation, discuss the field inspection findings and determine the next steps.
Environmental activist and architect Iqbal Habib identified Dhaka WASA's sewage and drainage system as one of the major sources of pollution.
“Dhaka's sewage is being discharged into the rivers through drains. There were plans to establish four sewage treatment plants in the capital,” he said.
The Dasherkandi Sewage Treatment Plant has been constructed, but questions remain over its effective utilization and the extent to which the city's sewage network is connected to treatment facilities.
Habib said the remaining planned facilities need to be implemented alongside a system to reconnect Dhaka's canals with surrounding rivers.
“Building treatment plants alone will not solve the problem. The canals need to be connected to the rivers and the entire drainage and sewage system has to be redesigned,” he said.
He also called for proposed river and canal projects to be made public for expert and citizen review.
“Otherwise, thousands of crores of taka may be spent without actually saving Dhaka's rivers,” he warned.
Shipping Ministry Secretary Md Zakaria said the survey was conducted through field inspections.
“Through the survey, 424 sources of waste discharge have been identified. Polluted liquid waste is entering the rivers through these outlets every day,” he said.
He said the relevant authorities had been notified and that a meeting with the Chief Adviser's Principal Secretary would be held to discuss measures against the identified sources.
Experts say the findings must be followed by enforcement, including mapping the outlets, identifying their owners, monitoring waste discharge and ensuring industries operate functional ETPs.
They also called for clearer accountability among the Department of Environment, WASA, city corporations, BIWTA, the Bangladesh Water Development Board and local government bodies.
Unless the identified sources are stopped, environmentalists say, efforts to clean the rivers will provide only temporary relief.
The committee's September 1 meeting is expected to determine the next steps for addressing the identified pollution sources and coordinating action among the agencies involved.

item.title: Local polls: BNP pushes single candidates as MPs build camps
item.description:
The ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) is pushing for single candidates in the upcoming local government elections, but growing competition among grassroots leaders and efforts by lawmakers to promote their own political camps are complicating the process.
In almost every Union Parishad, multiple BNP leaders are expressing interest in contesting the chairperson’s post. In some unions, three or four potential candidates are already preparing to enter the race.
In the Motobi Union of Feni Sadar Upazila, at least nine BNP leaders and supporters are currently interested in or actively preparing to contest the chairperson’s post.
Similar activities involving multiple potential candidates have been reported in many other unions across the country, raising concerns within the party that bringing unsuccessful contenders behind a single BNP-backed candidate could prove difficult once the election schedule is announced.
The BNP central leadership fears that multiple candidates could split the party vote and revive the internal conflicts seen during the national election, when rebel BNP candidates contested in 72 constituencies.
The effects of those rivalries are still visible in several areas. Party leaders fear that similar divisions in the local elections could undermine organisational unity and give Jamaat-e-Islami and other contenders an opportunity to gain ground.
Against this backdrop, BNP Chairman and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has repeatedly instructed party leaders, activists and lawmakers to remain united.
He has stressed the need to support one honest, competent, popular and acceptable candidate in each locality. He has also called for reducing tensions between party leaders and MPs and warned against fielding rebel candidates outside the party’s decision.
However, there is a clear gap between the central directive and the reality on the ground.
Even before the election schedule is announced, potential candidates have begun strengthening their positions through public outreach. Many are travelling to Dhaka to seek support from local MPs and maintain regular contact with them at Parliament, their offices and residences.
They believe an MP’s political influence in the constituency could play a significant role in the local elections.
A section of BNP grassroots leaders, however, is concerned about candidates being selected primarily on the basis of MPs’ preferences.
They fear that if lawmakers promote close associates or loyalists, leaders outside their camps may decide to contest independently, potentially splitting the BNP vote and triggering fresh conflicts at the local level.
BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi said the party has not yet issued any formal organisational directive regarding local-level candidacies.
However, he said Tarique Rahman has been instructing district and metropolitan leaders during consultation meetings to work for party unity and support single candidates.
BNP Joint Secretary General Emran Saleh Prince said: “The BNP will support those who have popularity and acceptability at the local level—that is our declared position.”
Party organisational leaders said local popularity, acceptability, organisational standing and past political activities would be taken into consideration when selecting candidates.
For Union Parishad elections, upazila-level leaders will play a role in the selection process, while district leaders will be involved in selecting candidates at the upazila level. Any disputes will initially be addressed at the district and divisional levels, with the central leadership intervening if necessary.
There is also concern within the party over the growing influence of MPs.
BNP Rajshahi Divisional Organising Secretary Syed Shaheen Shawkat said interference by lawmakers could become a cause for concern.
Emphasising that the party is bigger than any individual, he said the central leadership would be informed if any MP went too far in promoting his own camp or “own men”.
The lingering divisions from the national election are already affecting preparations in several constituencies, including Natore-1 and Mymensingh-11.
Supporters of incumbent MPs and followers of rebel candidates from the national election are seeking to field their preferred candidates in the local polls. Unless compromises are reached, multiple BNP candidates could enter the race in these areas.
The internal dynamics within the BNP have become even more significant as rival parties step up their activities ahead of the local elections.
Potential Jamaat-e-Islami candidates are already active in several areas. There is also discussion among BNP grassroots leaders that many leaders of the now-banned Awami League may seek to contest the elections as independents.
If the BNP vote is divided, rival candidates could directly benefit.
Meanwhile, the Election Commission plans to begin the local government election process with Union Parishad elections toward the end of the year.
Preparations are underway to announce the schedule by September. Of the roughly 4,500 Union Parishads across the country, the plan is to hold the first phase of voting in those eligible for elections.
According to the EC’s calculations, Union Parishad voting could begin toward the end of November.
Local Government Minister Dr Abdul Moin Khan said: “The government will provide 100% cooperation to the Election Commission in holding a free and fair election. Who wins or loses is not the government’s concern. The government wants to make the election acceptable and keep it free from political influence.”

item.title: Lionel Messi bids farewell to international football after 20-year journey
item.description:
Lionel Messi has announced his retirement from the Argentina national team, bringing an end to a 20-year international career that saw him lead La Albiceleste through one of the most successful eras in its history.
The 39-year-old captain confirmed his decision in an emotional farewell message, saying the choice was painful but that he felt the time had come to step away.
“After all this time since the final, and after thinking about it a lot, I want to tell everyone that I’m retiring from the national team,” Messi said.
“It was a decision that hurt and still hurts deep inside, but I understand that this is the right moment. I swear I always gave everything, not only in these last few years when we won everything, but before that too.”
Messi said he had always fought to bring joy to Argentina's supporters and make them proud through football.
“I always fought and gave everything for this shirt, to bring you happiness and make you feel proud to be Argentine through football,” he said.
The eight-time Ballon d'Or winner also pointed to the emergence of younger players as another reason to bring his international career to a close.
“There are great young players coming through who deserve to be here,” he said.
Thanking supporters for their backing over the past 20 years, Messi said he would now follow Argentina as a fan.
“Now I’ll be one of you, always supporting from the outside, in the good times and even more in the bad ones,” he said.
Messi leaves the national team after an extraordinary run that included the 2022 FIFA World Cup and consecutive Copa América titles. He also established himself as Argentina's all-time leading goalscorer during a career spanning more than 200 international appearances.
His decision comes after Argentina's defeat in the 2026 FIFA World Cup final and the recent death of his father, Jorge Messi, a loss that Messi referenced in explaining why he had become even more certain about his decision.
Messi is expected to continue his club career in Major League Soccer with Inter Miami, where he remains under contract.

item.title: Got waste? Exchange it for rice, oil, lentils
item.description:
Dhaka South City Corporation is turning recyclable waste into a form of currency, allowing residents to exchange discarded plastic and other materials for rice, lentils, cooking oil and other essentials in an initiative it plans to expand across all its wards within months.
The “Market in Exchange for Waste” program was launched in Hazaribagh’s Ward 55 on Monday, introducing an incentive-based approach that seeks to tackle two persistent urban problems at once, mounting waste and the economic pressure facing low-income communities.
Rather than treating residents merely as beneficiaries, the program seeks to make them participants in waste collection by attaching an immediate economic value to materials that would otherwise end up on streets, in drains or in landfills.
Following the inauguration, residents brought collected waste to temporary stalls and exchanged it for rice, lentils, cooking oil, salt, potatoes, tissue and other household essentials.
Dhaka South City Corporation Administrator Md Abdus Salam inaugurated the initiative at a field adjacent to a slum in Hazaribagh. The program is being implemented jointly with Bidyanondo Foundation.
DSCC Administrator Md Abdus Salam visits a stall during the launch of the `Market in Exchange for Waste` initiative in Ward 55 on Monday. Photo: Courtesy
The Hazaribagh launch is intended to be only the beginning. Salam said a permanent waste-exchange stall would be established in Gulistan within a week, while DSCC plans to establish one in each of its wards within the next three to four months.
“Active participation of citizens is crucial to building a clean city. ‘Market in Exchange for Waste’ is an effective model for encouraging such participation,” he said.
Under the model, recyclable waste collected by residents acquires an exchange value that can be redeemed for essential commodities.
The approach is particularly aimed at encouraging people in marginalized communities to collect and properly dispose of recyclable materials instead of allowing them to accumulate in neighbourhoods or enter the city’s drainage system.
Salam said plastic and other solid waste dumped into drains and sewers obstruct water flow, contributing to the chronic waterlogging that affects Dhaka during heavy rainfall.
Disposing of waste at designated locations, he said, could therefore help address both environmental pollution and waterlogging.
Bidyanondo Foundation Executive Director Jamal Uddin said the objective was to go beyond conventional assistance.
“We are not just helping marginalized people; we are making them partners in keeping the city clean,” he said.
The foundation’s previous experience suggests discarded plastic can have significant economic value when collected systematically.
According to Uddin, Bidyanondo generated around Tk1 crore from selling plastic waste over the past two years and used the proceeds to help provide meals to nearly 400,000 people.
The new initiative now seeks to scale up that model.
Organizers have set a target of collecting around 100,000kg of waste through 100 mobile campaigns over the next year.
The proposed permanent stalls could take the program further by creating regular collection points rather than relying solely on individual campaigns.
DSCC also plans to introduce another exchange-based initiative, “Food in Exchange for Books”, at suitable secondary transfer stations.
Under that program, spaces equipped with chairs, tables and books would be created for street children, combining food assistance with opportunities to read.
DSCC Chief Waste Management Officer Air Commodore Md Mahbubur Rahman Talukder, other senior city corporation officials and Bidyanondo Foundation volunteers attended Monday’s launch.

item.title: Rabbani’s studentship cancelled, Rashed declared 2019 Ducsu GS
item.description:
The Dhaka University Syndicate has cancelled the studentship of Golam Rabbani, former general secretary of the banned Bangladesh Chhatra League, and declared Rashed Khan general secretary (GS) of the Dhaka University Central Students’ Union (Ducsu), seven years and five months after the 2019 election.
Rabbani had been declared the winner of the GS post in the 2019 Ducsu election with 10,484 votes, while Rashed came second with 6,063 votes.
The decision came after the university’s Academic Council cancelled Rabbani’s studentship in its MPhil programme.
Rashed announced the development in a post on his verified Facebook page on Monday.
A former Dhaka University student, Rashed is currently serving as the political assistant to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.
In his Facebook post, Rashed wrote: “Alhamdulillah, Alhamdulillah, Alhamdulillah.”
He said a university-formed investigation committee had found Rabbani’s MPhil studentship to be invalid. Rabbani also failed to provide an appropriate response to a show-cause notice issued by the university syndicate, he said.
Following the cancellation of Rabbani’s studentship at a meeting of the Academic Council, his Ducsu position was also cancelled. The Syndicate then declared Rashed, who received the second-highest number of votes in the 2019 election, as GS.
The Ducsu election was held on March 11, 2019.
According to the results announced by the election commission, Nurul Haque Nur won the vice-president (VP) post with 11,062 votes.
His closest rival was Rezwanul Haque Chowdhury Shovon, then central president of Chhatra League, who received 9,129 votes.
Rabbani won the GS post with 10,484 votes, while Rashed came second with 6,063 votes.
Earlier, on November 26, 2025, the Academic Council cancelled Rabbani’s studentship in the MPhil programme and declared his position as Ducsu GS invalid.

item.title: Ducsu: Govt backtracking on July uprising promises
item.description:
Marking the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearance, the Dhaka University Central Students' Union (DUCSU) accused the government of backtracking on the promises for which the July uprising was fought.
The discussion, titled “Can You Hear?”, followed by a screening of the disappearance-themed film “Joar,” was held at the university’s RC Majumder Auditorium.
DUCSU Vice President Abu Shadik Kayem, who chaired the event, said the greatest gain of the July uprising was the return of many people who had been forcibly disappeared.
“But the government now in power is moving in a direction opposite to the Bangladesh we dreamed of after the July uprising,” he said.
“Through its student organization’s imposition of terror on campuses, it is essentially moving to relaunch the arrangements of the earlier fascist regime.”
Human rights activist and Drik Art Gallery founder Shahidul Alam spoke of the fear that history could repeat itself.
“May the horrifying time we lived through never return,” he said.
“After the July uprising, we thought the culture of disappearance and killing would never come back. But this government’s indifference terrifies us.”
He also spoke about his own experience of torture under the ousted government.
Nur Khan Liton, a human rights advocate and former head of Ain o Salish Kendra, said enforced disappearances could not be viewed as isolated incidents.
“Disappearances were carried out through the coordination of the entire state machinery,” he said.
He called on the government to ensure trials for enforced disappearances and other crimes against humanity committed during what he described as the fascist period.
Mohammad Tajul Islam, who until recently served as chief prosecutor of the International Crimes Tribunal, also addressed the gathering.
Among the speakers was Mir Ahmad Bin Quasem, MP for Dhaka-14 and a survivor of enforced disappearance under the previous regime.
He recounted his ordeal and called on the government to locate and return everyone who remains missing.
Nousheen Sharmila Ritu, a PhD researcher at the University of Warwick and former Oxford student, spoke about human rights and the scale of enforced disappearances in Bangladesh.
DUCSU Assistant General Secretary Md Muhiuddin Khan highlighted the mental health challenges faced by people who have returned after being disappeared.
He also criticized what he described as the government’s efforts to take the country back to the old system.
“The government is continuing its effort to take the country back to the old system, which is suicidal. If the government keeps this up, the people will give their answer too,” he said.
DUCSU executive member Md Shahinur Rahman, in his welcome remarks, raised concerns over bureaucratic hurdles faced by the families of victims and alleged that the government had failed to follow up with them.
Also present were DUCSU General Secretary S M Farhad and executive members Md Mazharul Islam, Arman Hossain, Iqbal Haider, Md Raisul Islam and Md Miftahul Hussain Al Maruf.
Fatima Tasnim Juma, DUCSU secretary for Liberation War and Democratic Movement Affairs, moderated the session.
Families of victims who remain missing also spoke at the event.
Abdul Halim, father of Al-Muqaddas, a former Islamic University student who disappeared and remains unaccounted for, renewed his appeal to the government to find his son.
Motiur Rahman, elder brother of Zaker Hussain, who was disappeared by state forces, said: “Even if it’s my brother’s dead body, we want him returned. This wait is no longer bearable.”
Ripon Hossain, brother of Rezwan Hossain, who also disappeared, made an emotional appeal to the government to bring his brother home.

item.title: Mahdi Amin terms China visit as successful, productive
item.description:
Prime Minister’s Education and Primary and Mass Education Adviser Dr Mahdi Amin has described the recent three-day visit to China as highly fruitful and successful, marked by the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on technical education, the inauguration of an international service center and the launch of three new institutional platforms.
He made the remarks on Monday in response to questions from journalists at a press conference on his post-China visit, held at the meeting room of the Technical and Madrasa Education Division of the Ministry of Education.
Dr Mahdi Amin said China has a reputation worldwide for providing quality technical education in a highly effective and cost-efficient manner.
He said that during the short visit led by Education and Primary and Mass Education Minister Dr A N M Ehsanul Hoque Milon, fruitful discussions were held with representatives of over 50 leading technical and vocational universities, institutes and industries in China.
“The key achievement of the visit is that a specific institutional foundation has been laid to enhance the skills of teachers and students in Bangladesh’s technical education sector,” he said.
He said that during the visit, a significant MoU titled “China-Bangladesh Vocational Education, Training and Research Center” was signed, while the “China-Bangladesh Industry and Education Integration International Service Center” was formally launched.
Besides, three more platforms were launched to strengthen joint cooperation. These are the “China-Bangladesh Vocational Teacher Training Center”, the “Bangladesh Vocational Education Research Center” and the “Bangladesh Chinese Language+ Skill Development Cooperation Center”.
The adviser said, “Ensuring rapid employment by upgrading the skills of our young people is one of the government’s key goals. Initiatives have been taken so that students can gain proficiency in the Chinese language and easily secure employment in domestic and international organizations.”
Education and Primary and Mass Education Minister Dr A N M Ehsanul Hoque Milon and Secretary of the Technical and Madrasah Education Division Md Daud Mia, along with senior officials of the ministry, were present at the press conference.

item.title: The Makkah defense pact and Bangladesh: A test of strategic autonomy
item.description:
From the Middle East to South Asia, the strategic map is changing rapidly. Prolonged wars, regional conflicts, economic uncertainty, and intensifying rivalry among major powers are prompting states to rethink how they secure their national interests.
One of the most significant recent developments is the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement, signed in Makkah on August 7, 2026 by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan. The agreement states that an armed attack against any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against all three, while also calling for broader defense cooperation.
For Bangladesh, the issue is no longer merely whether it should join the Makkah framework. The larger question is how Dhaka can develop a defense and foreign-policy strategy that maximizes its security options without becoming strategically dependent on any single power or drawn into conflicts unrelated to its national interests.
Recent statements from Bangladesh indicate that Dhaka is keeping the possibility of participation open. Foreign Affairs Adviser Humayun Kabir has said that Bangladesh views the possibility positively but would consider any such arrangement in light of its national interests and the changing global environment. This is not the same as a decision to join, but it makes the strategic debate increasingly relevant.
More than an “Islamic NATO”
The Makkah agreement has understandably been described in some quarters as an emerging “Islamic NATO.” Such a description, however, is premature. NATO possesses a highly developed institutional structure, integrated command arrangements, and decades of operational experience. The Makkah framework is at a much earlier stage.
Nevertheless, its political and strategic significance should not be underestimated. Saudi Arabia contributes enormous financial resources and considerable geopolitical influence; Türkiye brings a sophisticated and increasingly autonomous defense industry, NATO experience and advanced capabilities in drones, electronic warfare, and other military technologies; while Pakistan contributes a large and experienced military and nuclear capability.
The agreement therefore brings together three complementary sources of strategic power. If implemented effectively, it could eventually facilitate greater cooperation in defense production, military training, intelligence, technology transfer, and collective deterrence. Türkiye's foreign minister has also indicated that the pact is not directed against any particular country and that other states could potentially participate in the future.
Why now?
The emergence of the Makkah framework must be understood against a rapidly deteriorating regional security environment. The Israeli strike on Hamas leadership in Doha in 2025 demonstrated that even states traditionally viewed as relatively secure could find themselves exposed to the spillover effects of regional conflicts. Qatar, an important mediator between Israel and Hamas, condemned the strike as a violation of its sovereignty.
The subsequent escalation of regional tensions, including the 2026 Iran-related conflict and attacks affecting Gulf security, has reinforced the perception among regional powers that they cannot rely indefinitely on external security guarantees.
The Makkah initiative can therefore be interpreted partly as an effort to strengthen regional strategic autonomy. It does not necessarily represent a rejection of the United States or existing alliances. Rather, it reflects a broader trend in which regional powers seek greater capacity to manage their own security environment.
What could Bangladesh gain?
Bangladesh has legitimate reasons to examine the development carefully. Its defense capabilities remain significantly dependent on imported equipment and technology. Türkiye's growing defense industry could provide opportunities in drones, unmanned systems, naval platforms, electronic warfare, and defense manufacturing. Saudi Arabia offers financial strength and investment potential, while Pakistan has extensive military experience and established institutions for military education and training.
Bangladesh already maintains separate relationships with all three countries. Saudi Arabia is important to Bangladesh because of labour migration, remittances, investment, energy, and broader political and cultural ties. Türkiye is becoming an increasingly important economic and defense partner. Relations with Pakistan remain historically sensitive because of the legacy of 1971, but contemporary diplomatic, economic, educational, and military contacts have expanded.
A carefully designed engagement with the Makkah framework could therefore offer Bangladesh three potential advantages:
But these benefits must be weighed against substantial risks.
Bangladesh's security environment is different
The principal weakness of simply joining an existing security framework is that Bangladesh's security priorities are not identical to those of Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, or Pakistan.
Saudi Arabia's primary security concerns are centred on the Gulf and the wider Middle East. Pakistan's strategic calculations are deeply influenced by India, Afghanistan, and South Asian military competition. Türkiye's security environment encompasses Europe, the Black Sea, the Middle East, and its NATO commitments.
Bangladesh's priorities are different: Relations with India, the Bay of Bengal, the situation in Myanmar and Rakhine, border security, maritime trade routes, the Indian Ocean, and emerging climate-related security challenges.
Consequently, Bangladesh should not automatically adopt another country's threat perceptions as its own.
This distinction is particularly important because of the collective-defense provision. If Bangladesh were to become a formal member of a pact under which an attack on Pakistan could potentially trigger obligations toward Pakistan, India's assessment of Bangladesh's strategic orientation would inevitably change. Defense cooperation with Türkiye is one thing; participation in a collective-defense arrangement involving Pakistan is strategically much more consequential.
Managing India, China, and the United States
India would naturally watch any Bangladeshi move toward the Makkah framework closely. Bangladesh therefore needs to avoid creating the perception that its defense policy is being directed against India.
China would also have strong reasons to monitor developments. Pakistan is one of Beijing's closest strategic partners, while China maintains substantial economic and diplomatic relations with Türkiye and Saudi Arabia. Bangladesh itself is an important Chinese economic and defense partner. Greater Bangladeshi diversification of defense relationships could therefore encourage Beijing to strengthen rather than reduce its engagement with Dhaka.
Washington would view the development through the wider lens of the Indo-Pacific. Bangladesh's strategic location along the Bay of Bengal makes its foreign and defense policies relevant to maritime security and the wider Indo-Pacific balance.
This is where Bangladesh's diplomatic skill will be tested.
From weapons buyer to technology partner
The most important lesson for Bangladesh is that defense diplomacy should not be reduced to purchasing weapons.
Buying fighter aircraft from one country, drones from another, and missiles from a third may diversify suppliers, but it does not necessarily create strategic autonomy. Bangladesh could remain a permanent consumer in the global arms market.
A more ambitious objective would be to acquire technology, production capability, and knowledge.
Bangladesh should explore joint development and local production of drones and unmanned systems, military electronics, surveillance equipment, communications systems, and selected naval technologies. Cooperation with Türkiye could be particularly valuable in this regard. Defense-industrial cooperation can also stimulate research, skilled employment, technological innovation, and broader industrial development.
The strategic question should therefore change from “Where can Bangladesh buy weapons?” to “How can Bangladesh become a partner in developing and producing defense technology?”
A better option: Diversified defense diplomacy
For Bangladesh, the most realistic strategy may be diversified and issue-based defense cooperation rather than membership in a rigid military bloc.
Dhaka can deepen defense-technology cooperation with Türkiye; expand investment, training and maritime-security cooperation with Saudi Arabia; maintain selective military education, training, and peacekeeping cooperation with Pakistan; continue appropriate defense and technological cooperation with China; pursue maritime surveillance and advanced technological cooperation with the United States and European partners; and maintain pragmatic security cooperation with India on border management, maritime affairs, counterterrorism, and regional stability.
Such an approach would maximize Bangladesh's options while minimizing dependence.
Three principles should guide any future defense agreement.
First , Bangladesh should avoid joining a military alliance explicitly directed against another state.
Second , Bangladeshi territory should never become a foreign military base or a platform for military operations against another country.
Third , Bangladesh should avoid excessive dependence on any single country's weapons, technology or defense infrastructure.
A fourth principle is equally important: Before entering any major security agreement, Bangladesh must assess not only the immediate military benefits but also the economic costs, diplomatic consequences, and potential obligations that could arise during a future conflict.
Strategic autonomy, not strategic isolation
The Makkah Joint Defense Agreement could become an important new element in the security architecture of the Middle East and the wider Muslim world. Whether it remains a limited trilateral arrangement or evolves into a broader regional framework is still uncertain. What is clear, however, is that the agreement has opened a new strategic conversation.
Bangladesh should therefore watch the initiative closely rather than rush toward membership. If a formal proposal for participation emerges, Dhaka should evaluate its precise obligations, military benefits, economic costs, and diplomatic consequences before making a decision.
Bangladesh's national interest would not be served by entering an arrangement in which another country's war automatically becomes Bangladesh's war.
The country's strategic objective should instead be strategic autonomy without strategic isolation.
Bangladesh's greatest strategic asset is not a fighter aircraft, missile, or military alliance. It is geography. Situated at the intersection of South Asia and Southeast Asia and facing the Bay of Bengal, Bangladesh occupies a position of exceptional strategic importance.
If that geographical advantage is combined with effective diplomacy, economic strength, technological capacity, and credible national defense, Bangladesh can become not a follower of another country's security architecture but an influential regional actor in its own right.
The goal, therefore, should not be to choose one camp over another. It should be to build a network of partnerships in which different countries cooperate with Bangladesh in different areas, while Bangladesh retains the freedom to determine when, where, and how its national interests require engagement.
Dr Nasir Uddin Ahmed is a retired Major, researcher and political/security analyst. Email: directtoradmin2007@gmail.com .

item.title: Court issues warrant against Lakeshore Hotel MD Kazi Tareq Shams in fraud case
item.description:
A Dhaka court has issued a warrant against Lakeshore Hotel managing director Kazi Tareq Shams and his associate MA Masud on charges of breach of trust and fraud.
Judge Mohammad Hossain Muhammad Jonayed of Dhaka's Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court No. 4 issued the order on August 31.
The case alleges that Kazi Tareq Shams, with the help of his associate MA Masud, fraudulently registered Lakeshore Hotel shares in their own names, taking advantage of the frail condition of his father Kazi Shamsul Haque, who was suffering from old age-related illness and amnesia.
The victim's siblings filed a case in court regarding this incident.
The plaintiff's lawyer Barrister Al Mamun Rasel said: "The defendants, in collusion with each other, took advantage of their father's illness and fraudulently registered all the shares in their own names to deprive the heirs. The CID investigated the case twice and submitted a report to the court finding the primary truth of the fraud.”
“After reviewing the report and documents, the court took cognizance of the case and issued summons against the defendants. And after issuing the summons, the defendants did not appear in court, so the court issued a farewell warrant. We believe that through this order, the plaintiff has made important progress on the path to justice,” he added.
Despite repeated attempts, Kazi Tareq Shams could not be reached for a comment.
The court mentioned in its order that the preliminary truth of the crimes under sections 406 (breach of trust), 420 (cheating) and 109 (incitement/aiding) of the Penal Code against the defendants was found in the investigation report and the review of the relevant documents.
As a result, the court accepted the investigation report, took the case into consideration for trial and ordered the issuance of summons against the two defendants.
After issuing the summons and the accused did not appear before the learned court, the court issued a warrant.

item.title: Eight injured as bus overturns on Padma Bridge
item.description:
Eight people were seriously injured after a Dhaka-bound passenger bus lost control and overturned on the Mawa-end slope of the Padma Bridge in Munshiganj on Monday afternoon.
The accident disrupted traffic on the Dhaka-bound lane for nearly 45 minutes before the overturned bus was removed and the road was cleared.
Muhammad Shofiqul Islam, deputy assistant director of Munshiganj Fire Service and Civil Defence, said the “New Green Line Express” bus was travelling to Dhaka from Magura when the accident occurred.
He said the bus lost control due to excessive speed while descending the bridge, hit the roadside railing and overturned.
Two rescue teams from Sreenagar Fire Station soon arrived and rescued the injured passengers from the bus.
The injured were taken to Sreenagar Upazila Health Complex in fire service ambulances.
The injured were identified as Saifullah, 80; Md Lutfar, 63; Rebeka Khatun, 40; Nur Islam, 46; Rashida, 40; Fatema, 7; Saif, 23; and Arafat, 13.

item.title: Nepali teacher saved hundreds of students from flood, minutes before it arrived
item.description:
Hundreds of Nepali schoolchildren were saved by their teacher shortly before the school was inundated in last week’s devastating floods.
A Trishuli local, Surinder, said the floods “swept away the entire building.”
“Here used to be a three-story school building in front of a temple and there was a market nearby,” Surinder said.
“When floods hit this area, the teacher evacuated all the students and saved their lives.”
Surinder said Rajendra Dawadi, who is head teacher at Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School in Nuwakot, saved the lives of about 1,600 students.
Mr Dawadi told the BBC he received calls warning of the incoming disaster.
“If we didn’t make a quick decision, if it were 10 minutes later, we all, including the students and me, wouldn’t be able to speak to you today,” he told the BBC.
“A parent came and told me that ‘a big flood was coming, I am here to take my daughter, I will take her.’
“Parents don’t rush without a strong reason, so it was confirmed that I shouldn’t waste a second to evacuate the children.
“I decided I shouldn’t delay any more. Even if the flood was not coming, it was just a matter of a single day’s classes.
“I feel proud that we saved so many lives.”
In one of the areas worst hit by the floods, at another school, a group of schoolchildren survived when they left their classroom for lunch.
Children attending other classes at the Shree Bagheswori Madhyamik School in Galchhi also escaped because teachers told them to quickly evacuate their classrooms shortly before the waters came crashing in.
“The teachers said, ‘There is a flood, and you should leave bags and tiffins [lunch boxes],’” Lakshmi Shrestha, the mother of a student attending the school, said.
“That’s how they managed to survive.”
Shrestha was among the mothers and children who began returning to their school on Sunday to find the kids’ belongings and see what could be salvaged.
The majority of the children at the school appeared to have survived the floods, the families said.
Thick brown and grey mud coated the surfaces of school benches, walls and notebooks, while the school’s courtyard was filled with sediment.
Lines on the walls showed how quickly the water rose.
A pile of small mud-caked backpacks, some with colorful key chains, were on the benches and floors, waiting to be claimed.
Kopila Mizar, a student’s mother, couldn’t find her son’s backpack but remained positive.
“My son is alive; that is my biggest happiness,”
she said.
At least 69 schools in Nepal’s flood-devastated districts have been destroyed or damaged, putting education at risk for nearly 19,000 children, according to the non-profit Save the Children.
Those numbers are likely to rise as rescue teams reach more areas, they said.
The government ordered schools and universities to shut down for three days following torrential rains that triggered severe flash floods and landslides across parts of the country.
University exams were also paused.
With communities still receiving constant flood warnings advising them to move to higher, safer areas, it’s unclear when classes can resume.
The disaster has killed more than 900 people, and more than 4,200 people are unaccounted for in Nepal, according to the latest figures released by the Nepal police.
Chinese authorities said 16 people were killed in Gyirong County, Tibet, and 546 are missing.

item.title: PM: BNP wants to repay people’s love by establishing accountable state
item.description:
Prime Minister and BNP Chairman Tarique Rahman on Monday said his party wants to repay the people’s love by establishing an accountable state.
In a message marking BNP’s 48th founding anniversary, he also said the people once again entrusted BNP with the task of running the state through a free, fair and neutral election after the end of one-and-a-half decades of fascist rule and exploitation.
“BNP wants to repay the people’s love by establishing an accountable state. With this goal, the BNP government is working tirelessly to establish Bangladesh as a welfare state,” Tarique Rahman said.
He urged BNP leaders, activists, supporters and well-wishers to continue dedicating themselves to serving the country while maintaining the people’s trust and confidence.
The Prime Minister greeted the people of Bangladesh as well as BNP leaders, activists, supporters and well-wishers on the party’s 48th founding anniversary, describing the occasion as a source of joy, enthusiasm and inspiration for the people.
BNP was founded by then President Ziaur Rahman on September 1, 1978.
Recalling the party’s founding, Tarique Rahman said its establishment was a landmark event in the history of restoring democracy in Bangladesh.
He said Ziaur Rahman restored democracy after assuming the responsibility of running the country and restored the right of banned political parties to conduct politics.
“BNP was established in response to the needs of the time. As a result, a new journey towards pluralistic democracy began in Bangladesh,” the Prime Minister said.
He paid tribute to Ziaur Rahman, whom he described as the proclaimer of independence, successful statesman and architect of modern Bangladesh.
Tarique Rahman also remembered former Prime Minister and BNP Chairperson Khaleda Zia, saying she took BNP to every household in Bangladesh through her charismatic personality and leadership.
He said his party also played the role of a vigilant guardian in protecting the country’s independence and sovereignty while standing alongside the people. “Whenever the country’s independence, sovereignty and democracy came under threat, BNP leaders, supporters and well-wishers sacrificed their lives alongside the pro-democracy people,” he said.
The BNP chief also paid tribute to BNP leaders and activists at all levels who had been killed or injured in the struggle to establish democracy and good governance in the country.
He said BNP was allowed to govern whenever people were able to cast their votes freely in fair elections.
During its various terms in office, Tarique Rahman said BNP governments took important initiatives to strengthen and institutionalise democracy, including restoring the parliamentary system and expanding women’s education.
He said BNP’s efforts and initiatives to uphold democracy and achieve economic prosperity made it the country’s most popular political party.
“BNP believes that the pro-democracy people of Bangladesh are the source of all its political power. BNP is synonymous with the struggle to build a welfare-oriented, democratic and self-reliant Bangladesh,” he said.

item.title: UGC to raise PhD scholarships to 500 next year
item.description:
The University Grants Commission (UGC) plans to increase the number of its PhD scholarships fivefold to 500 from the next fiscal year to help address the shortage of qualified university teachers and strengthen research capacity in the country.
UGC Chairman Professor Dr Mamun Ahmed announced the plan at the commission’s 179th full meeting on Monday.
He said the number of UGC-funded PhD scholarships had already increased from 75 to 100, and the commission now plans to raise it to 500 from the next fiscal year.
The commission has also increased opportunities for PhD studies abroad from 10 to 35, while it is working to expand postdoctoral fellowship opportunities.
The UGC will further propose a special government allocation for PhD and postdoctoral research in the next fiscal year, Mamun Ahmed said.
He said expanding opportunities for both domestic and overseas PhD studies was necessary to address the shortage of qualified teachers at universities.
The UGC chairman also stressed the need to develop skilled researchers, modern research infrastructure and sustainable research funding, while encouraging greater collaboration between Bangladeshi and international researchers.
He called for university research to be more closely linked to real-world problems, industry and the economy through stronger university-industry partnerships and joint research initiatives.
Future research funding would be more strategic and results-oriented, with priority given to universities that make effective contributions to research, innovation and the knowledge-based economy, he added.
The commission also approved the UGC Promotional and Academic Staff Development Research Project Policy, 2026 at the meeting.
UGC members Professor Dr Masuma Habib, Professor Md Mehedi Hasan Khan, Professor Dr Md Aslam Hossain and Professor Dr Niaz Ahmed Chowdhury, along with vice-chancellors of different universities and relevant UGC officials, attended the meeting.

item.title: Belly fat linked to higher risk of dementia
item.description:
Belly fat is often associated with heart disease, diabetes, and high blood pressure, but recent research suggests it may also have a long-term negative effect on brain health, potentially raising the risk of dementia.
According to experts, visceral fat — the fat that accumulates deep around the liver, pancreas, and intestines — causes chronic inflammation, hormonal imbalance, and various metabolic problems in the body.
Over time, this can contribute to memory loss, reduced attention span, declining cognitive ability, and a higher risk of dementia.
A study published in the journal Immune Network said the gut does more than digest food: it plays an important role in the immune system, metabolism, and nervous system function.
Beneficial microorganisms in the gut, known as the gut microbiome, also help maintain brain health.
Researchers say not all body fat carries equal risk. Compared to subcutaneous fat, which sits under the skin, visceral fat is considerably more dangerous, since it releases inflammatory chemicals that can damage blood vessels, insulin function, and brain cells.
This reduces blood flow to the brain and disrupts normal communication between nerve cells.
The effects can include weakened memory, reduced attention span, slower thinking, difficulty learning new things, and declining cognitive ability.
Multiple studies have found that people with a larger waist circumference in midlife face a comparatively higher risk of developing Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia later in life.
The impact is not limited to physical health. Excess belly fat has also been linked to anxiety, depression, sleep problems, fatigue, and low energy.
Experts say inflammatory compounds released by this fat can disrupt the balance of key neurotransmitters in the brain, such as serotonin and dopamine.
Risk factors for visceral fat accumulation include calorie-dense processed foods, soft drinks, physical inactivity, insufficient sleep, chronic stress, smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, and aging.
Even people with a normal body weight can accumulate harmful fat inside the abdomen, which is why experts consider waist circumference, not just body weight, an important indicator of overall health.
Experts recommend regular exercise, a balanced diet, seven to nine hours of sleep per night, stress management, and regular health checkups as effective ways to reduce visceral fat.
These measures can lower the risk of heart disease and diabetes while also helping preserve brain function and memory over the long term.c

item.title: How to make paneer pulao at home
item.description:
Pulao is a staple of festive spreads, and few versions bring together comfort and flavor quite like paneer pulao — a dish built on soft paneer, fragrant whole spices, ghee, and basmati rice.
The dish is simple enough for a weeknight dinner but distinctive enough to serve guests.
To prepare it, start by washing two cups of basmati rice and soaking it in water for 20 to 30 minutes, then draining it.
Cut 250 grams of paneer into medium cubes and lightly fry them in oil until golden, then set aside.
In a separate pot, heat two tablespoons of ghee with one tablespoon of oil, and add a bay leaf, two cinnamon sticks, three cardamom pods, three to four cloves, and half a teaspoon of cumin seeds.
Once the spices release their aroma, add two thinly sliced onions and fry until lightly browned.
Next, add one teaspoon each of ginger and garlic paste along with three to four green chilies, and stir well. Add fried cashews and raisins, and cook briefly to build flavor.
Once the spices are well cooked, add the soaked rice and fry gently for two to three minutes over medium heat. Pour in about three cups of hot water, season with salt to taste, cover, and let it cook.
Once the water comes to a boil, gently fold in the fried paneer along with half a teaspoon of garam masala. When the water has nearly evaporated, lower the heat completely, cover the pot, and let the rice steam for eight to 10 minutes.
After turning off the heat, leave the lid on for another five minutes without opening it — this helps the rice turn out fluffy and lets the spices settle evenly.
To serve, uncover the pot and gently fluff the rice with a fork. Garnish with a touch of ghee, fried onions, or cilantro, and serve hot.
Paneer pulao pairs well with raita, salad, or chutney for a complete meal.

item.title: Standard Chartered Bangladesh appoints Enamul Huque as CEO
item.description:
Standard Chartered Bangladesh announced the appointment of Enamul Huque as chief executive officer, effective September 1, 2026.
Enam brings extensive leadership experience across corporate and institutional banking and risk management.
During his 25 years with Standard Chartered, both in Bangladesh and other markets, Enam has built deep expertise across local corporates, commodity trading and agribusiness, global subsidiaries and financial institutions; while leading strategic client relationships and landmark transactions across diverse sectors.
Reacting to his appointment, Enamul Huque, CEO, Standard Chartered Bangladesh, said: “It is an honour to be appointed as the CEO for Standard Chartered Bangladesh. This bank has been my professional identity for over 25 years. Taking up the role of chief executive officer of our Bangladesh franchise is both a recognition, and a big responsibility. My priority will be to continue to be the super connector international bank, invested in the success of our clients and regulators; and to remain the trusted partner to our clients, communities and other stakeholders.”
Immediately prior to his appointment as CEO, Enam served as country chief risk officer and senior credit officer from April 2025, overseeing risk across the Bangladesh franchise; and ensuring alignment with regulatory requirements and the bank’s growth ambitions.
He also chaired the bank’s Diversity and Inclusion Council.
Beyond his role at Standard Chartered, Enam has contributed to the broader development of Bangladesh’s financial sector.
He served as co-chair of the standing committee on capital markets and bond at the Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FBCCI) for the 2023 to 2025 term.
Enam holds an MBA from Mount Eliza Business School, Monash University, Australia; and graduate and post graduate degrees from the University of Dhaka.
Outside work, he enjoys travelling and has a keen appreciation for the arts.

item.title: AIUB hosts exhibition showcasing students’ animation, AR and digital creativity
item.description:
The Animation Track of the Department of Journalism and Mass Communication (JMC) at American International University-Bangladesh (AIUB) inaugurated “Beyond the Frame: Stories in Augmented Reality,” a three-day exhibition showcasing the creative works of students from the Animation and Journalism Tracks.
The exhibition was inaugurated on August 23 at AIUB.
The exhibition features students’ creative works in augmented reality (AR), animation, digital art, and interactive storytelling, including AR experiences inspired by AIUB student organizations, as well as the landscapes, people, and stories of Dhaka.
Selected virtual reality (VR) and other technology-based demonstrations are also being showcased.
The opening ceremony was graced by Nina P Cainglet, Ambassador of the Philippines to Bangladesh, as guest of honor.
Among the distinguished guests present were Hasanul A Hasan, founder member, board of trustees; Dr Carmen Z Lamagna, member, board of trustees and former vice chancellor of AIUB; Prof Saiful Islam, vice chancellor of AIUB; Prof Tazul Islam, dean, Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences (FASS).
Ambassador Nina P Cainglet highlighted the growing importance of the creative industries and the Philippines’ significant contribution to the global animation sector.
She noted that the Philippines has established itself as a trusted center for animation, particularly in digital and interactive media, and referred to the country’s Philippine Creative Industries Development Act as an important framework for nurturing and strengthening the creative sector.
The Ambassador further expressed her hope that the exhibition would mark the beginning of many more creative journeys and international collaborations between Bangladesh and the Philippines.
Hasanul A. Hasan, founder member of AIUB and member of the board of trustees, emphasized the importance of embracing emerging academic disciplines and preparing students for new opportunities in the rapidly changing, creative, and technology-driven economy.
Carmen Z Lamagna, member of the board of trustees and former vice chancellor of AIUB, highlighted the enormous potential of the animation industry and informed the audience about AIUB’s forthcoming initiative to establish a new academic department focused on animation.
Rani Elen V Ramos, lecturer, Animation Track, JMC, expressed her appreciation to the university authorities, faculty members, students, and collaborators for supporting the exhibition and creating a platform where young animators could present their work and explore new forms of storytelling.
In closing remarks, Prof Pradip Kumar Panday, head of JMC, congratulated the students, faculty members, and organizers for successfully bringing the exhibition to life.
The exhibition reflects JMC’s growing emphasis on hands-on learning, emerging media technologies, and interdisciplinary creative practice.
Through the Animation Track, students are encouraged to explore animation, augmented reality, virtual reality, digital storytelling, and other innovative forms of communication while developing the skills needed to thrive in the rapidly expanding global creative economy.
Associate Dean Faria Sultana; Prof Pradip Kumar Panday, head, Department of Journalism and Mass Communication; Prof Manzur H Khan, proctor; faculty members from JMC and other departments; administrative officials; advisers; guests; media representatives; and students were also present at the event.

item.title: Japanese automakers Nissan and Honda join forces on car software
item.description:
Japanese automakers Nissan and Honda have agreed to jointly develop computer components and software for vehicles expected to enter the market in fiscal 2029, the companies said Monday.
Under the agreement, Yokohama-based Nissan and Tokyo-based Honda will share standardized components for core electronic control units, or ECUs, as well as software.
The two companies began discussions in 2024 on cooperation in electric vehicles and automotive intelligence technology. Their latest agreement focuses on software-defined vehicles, whose functions and features can be controlled and updated through software rather than hardware. The announcement did not mention specific vehicle models or electric vehicles.
The global auto industry is increasingly shifting toward technologies such as automated driving, electrification and zero-emission vehicles, making cars more dependent on electronic systems and software.
The companies said sharing components and jointly conducting research could reduce costs, speed up development and create greater efficiency through large-scale production.
European automakers Volkswagen, BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Stellantis are also cooperating on software development and shared operating systems.
Nissan and Honda, both smaller than industry leader Toyota Motor Corp. in Japan, believe closer cooperation could strengthen their competitiveness.
The companies said they would also explore cooperation in areas including zero-emission technology and reducing traffic deaths.
Both stressed that faster development, efficient investment, electrification and intelligent vehicle technology would remain key priorities of their strategic partnership.

item.title: BNP, Chhatra Dal leaders jailed over gold snatching in airport area
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Monday sent two leaders of the BNP and its student wing, Chhatra Dal, to jail in a case filed over the snatching of gold jewelry in Dhaka airport area.
The court also fixed Tuesday for hearing their bail petitions.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Md Hasan Shahadat passed the order after the accused were produced before the court following a one-day remand. Abu Bakkar, a sub-inspector of the Prosecution Department, confirmed the matter.
The accused are Al-Amin Hasan Shanto, general secretary of the Airport Thana unit of Chhatra Dal, and Md Abdur Rouf, president of the Airport unit of BNP.
Kamrul Hasan, officer-in-charge of Airport Police Station, told Dhaka Tribune that the two were produced before the court on Monday after completing their one-day remand.
The court had earlier granted police one day’s remand for each of them after investigators sought three days to question them.
The incident took place on the night of August 28 in front of Balaka Bhaban on the Dhaka-Mymensingh Highway in the Airport area.
On August 29, Md Sumon filed a case with Airport Police Station over the incident.
Police later analyzed CCTV footage and conducted an operation to arrest people allegedly involved in the incident.
On August 30, investigating officer Sub-Inspector Sabbir Hossain produced the accused before the court and sought three days’ remand. The court granted one day’s remand for each.
After the remand period ended, the investigating officer sought an order to keep the accused in jail.
In the application, the investigating officer said the accused had provided information about the incident during interrogation, which was still being verified.
The application also said there was a strong possibility that the accused could go into hiding and hamper the investigation if released on bail.
The investigating officer therefore sought their detention in jail in the interest of a proper investigation and justice.
At Monday’s hearing, defense lawyer Abdul Rahman sought time for the bail petitions to be heard on Tuesday. The court subsequently sent the accused to jail and fixed Tuesday for the bail hearing.
According to the First Information Report (FIR), the complainant said his elder brother, Kawsar, is an expatriate living in Malaysia.
On August 28, Kawsar sent 200 grams of gold jewelry from Malaysia for his sister’s wedding and family use.
Later that evening, around 8pm, the complainant and his friend Rohan Chowdhury collected the jewelry from an acquaintance of Kawsar at the airport.
They then traveled in a rented microbus and got off opposite Balaka Bhaban on the Dhaka-Mymensingh Highway.
The FIR says the accused allegedly surrounded them as soon as they got out of the microbus and beat them after accusing them of being involved in Awami League and Chhatra League politics.
The accused also allegedly claimed that the two were carrying bombs.
At one point, the accused allegedly snatched the 200 grams of gold jewelry and fled the scene.
The FIR says the accused quickly left the area as people began gathering at the scene.
The FIR names four people as accused: Abdur Rouf, 40, president of the Airport unit of BNP; Ripon, 27, president of the Airport Thana unit of JCD; Al-Amin Shanto, 27, general secretary of the Airport Thana unit of JCD; and Rubel, 32, general secretary of an Airport ward unit of BNP.

item.title: Teacher’s death in snatching: Three placed on remand
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Monday placed three men on five-day remand each in a case filed over the death of primary school headteacher Ranjila Parveen, 56, who fell from an autorickshaw after snatchers grabbed her bag near the south plaza of the National Parliament.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Md Siddique Azad passed the order following a petition by the investigating officer.
The accused are Poni, alias Para Poni, alias Poni Gazi; Cedric Julian; and Rakib Hossain.
Sub-Inspector Shahin of Sher-e-Bangla Nagar police station, also the investigating officer in the case, produced the three accused before the court and sought a 10-day remand.
Lawyers Amir Uddin Amir and Shahadat Hossain Mamun, representing the accused, sought bail and urged the court to reject the remand plea.
During the hearing, the defense lawyers said the accused were not connected to the incident and urged the court to ensure that the actual perpetrators were brought to justice.
“We want the real culprits to be tried. No innocent person should be harassed,” they said.
They also claimed that the motorcycle identified in connection with the case did not match the one used to arrest the accused and alleged that the case was being diverted in another direction.
The court, however, granted five days’ remand for each of the accused.
Speaking to reporters after the hearing, Poni denied any involvement in the incident.
“We are not connected to this incident. The truth will prevail. RAB is fake. AI cameras are everywhere now, so we are not afraid. Allah will do something about this,” he said.
RAB-2 arrested the three men during an operation on Sunday and seized a Yamaha R15 motorcycle allegedly used in the snatching.
According to the case statement, Parveen was the headteacher of Bagbari Government Primary School in Gabtoli upazila of Bogra.
At around 5:55am on August 29, she was traveling by auto-rickshaw with her husband, Md Abdul Matin, to see an eye doctor.
When they were on the paved road near Gate 12 of the National Parliament on Manik Mia Avenue, snatchers riding a motorcycle grabbed her bag and pulled it forcefully.
The force of the pull caused Parveen to fall from the moving auto-rickshaw onto the paved road, leaving her with a severe head injury.
She was taken in critical condition to Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital and later to Dhaka Medical College Hospital, but doctors declared her dead on the way.
Her husband filed the case at Sher-e-Bangla Nagar police station on Sunday.
