item.title: Saving the Sundarbans from criminality
item.description:
The reopening of the Sundarbans is welcome news for thousands of fishermen, forest workers, and others whose livelihoods depend on the forest. It is unfortunate to note, thus, that piracy has once again become a serious threat in the area.
While many finally have an opportunity to return to work after three months of closure, and begin recovering from the financial strain that has accumulated in their absence, returning to the forest also means returning to fear.
Fishermen have reported being forced to pay extortion money to criminal groups in exchange for so-called tokens or slips that supposedly allow them to enter particular parts of the forest safely. Those who refuse can face abduction, assault and ransom demands.
For some locals, the threat from pirates has become more frightening than the forest's natural dangers.
This is unacceptable; people should not have to choose between risking their lives and abandoning their livelihoods.
These communities already live with poverty, debt, and the uncertainties of climate and nature. The return of organized criminal groups should not add another burden to their lives.
There have been encouraging efforts: Recent Coast Guard operations have resulted in arrests, weapons seizures, and the rescue of hostages, while several groups and their members have surrendered.
But sporadic successes cannot substitute for sustained security. Authorities must intensify coordinated patrols, intelligence gathering, and surveillance throughout the forest and its waterways.
Law enforcement agencies must also establish reliable channels through which fishermen can report threats without fearing retaliation.
Most importantly, those who finance, organize, and participate in these criminal networks must face justice.
The Sundarbans belongs to the nation, but its protection is inseparable from protecting the people who depend on it. A forest cannot truly be considered secure when the communities entering it for their livelihoods remain unsafe.
Making the Sundarbans safe for all who depend on it must be treated as a priority.

item.title: Matching environmental responsibility at home
item.description:
As a country that contributes comparatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions yet remains highly vulnerable to climate change, Bangladesh's demands for greater climate finance, adaptation support, and accountability from major emitters are both justified and necessary.
Yet despite being among the strongest voices for climate justice on the international stage, the latest Environmental Performance Index (EPI) offers an uncomfortable reminder: Climate leadership abroad must be matched by environmental responsibility at home.
Bangladesh ranks 175th out of 177 countries in the EPI 2026, with a score of 23.46 out of 100, and a particularly poor performance in air quality and ecosystem vitality.
Our rivers continue to suffer from industrial waste, sewage, plastic, and encroachment. Wetlands are disappearing under unplanned urbanization, while Dhaka's air remains dangerously polluted by vehicle emissions, construction dust, and other sources.
These are environmental concerns that directly affect public health, livelihoods, productivity, and the quality of life of millions.
Most concerning, however, is that Bangladesh does not necessarily lack policies or laws. The greater problem is implementation. Environmental regulations mean little when industries can evade pollution controls, wetlands can be filled, rivers can be occupied, and waste can be dumped with limited consequences.
Stronger enforcement, institutional coordination, and accountability are therefore essential.
This should also be viewed as an issue of climate justice: The right to clean air, safe water, and a healthy environment cannot be separated from the climate justice Bangladesh advocates for internationally. Protecting vulnerable communities and restoring damaged ecosystems must become central to national development.
Ultimately, we should continue demanding greater responsibility from the international community, but we must also demonstrate that responsibility ourselves.
Bangladesh's credibility as a climate champion will depend not only on what it says at global conferences, but on whether its citizens can also see and breathe the difference at home.

item.title: The reality of revolutions
item.description:
Facilitating the legacy of civil movements is challenging for both organizers and the public trying to change established autocratic governments. One major challenge after such movements is gaining trust and support for the new political system among citizens and various groups, both locally and internationally.
To address this, it is essential to build legitimacy, create effective government structures, and develop a sense of ownership among the people. It is also important to engage with international organizations to get recognition and support for the transition process.
The main structural issue is the struggle for power and leadership that follows an autocratic regime's collapse. When a former government falls apart, it creates a power vacuum. This can cause different revolutionary groups to split and compete with one another, leading to ideological fragmentation within the movement spirit.
The worrying factor is that without unity, there may be internal conflicts or a worrying shift back to authoritarian rule, both of which run counter to the movement's short- and long-term goals.
Karl Marx posited that revolutions arise from the intrinsic contradictions and conflicts embedded within class structures, particularly the antagonism between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat. As socio-economic inequalities intensify, the disenfranchised class mobilizes to dismantle the existing capitalist framework and establish a new socio-political paradigm.
Marx, in addition, argued that the inherent conflicts between social classes, notably between capitalists and workers, and the ensuing struggles for power, are fundamentally rooted in the unequal distribution of wealth and resources. This dynamic sets the stage for class consciousness to develop, ultimately driving revolutionary change in response to systemic oppression to avoid alienation from society.
Vladimir Lenin's Vanguard theory can also be understood in relation to the classification between movement and revolution. He stressed the importance of an organized group of revolutionaries to lead the working class in achieving socialism.
Although the July-August 2024 movement in Bangladesh did not reflect the spirit of the socialist movement, these theories played out during the expected 2024 upsurge, highlighting the relationship between organized movements and the public. It could offer insights into how effective a vanguard can be in gathering support, addressing social and economic problems, and promoting political change in Bangladesh.
Lenin’s Vanguard theory suggests that workers, or in Bangladesh's case, students, needed guidance to develop revolutionary awareness. This highlights the need for a well-disciplined revolutionary political party, which was absent during the movement in Bangladesh and is highly unlikely to emerge in the future.
Crane Brinton stated in “ The Anatomy of Revolution ” that the challenge of establishing a lasting order from the aftermath of a revolution frequently results in internal conflict and ultimately authoritarian rule. In his observation, Brinton likely noted that creating a new, stable system after a revolution can be challenging when the previous one has collapsed.
I have observed that differing perspectives and vested interests among societal factions can significantly complicate the rebuilding of the nation’s socio-economic and socio-political institutions in a spirit of democracy, even though the democratic process does not always yield ultimate success for nation-states.
These divergent views frequently result in conflicts that escalate over time. In such scenarios, it is not uncommon for a singular leader or faction to amass disproportionate power to reestablish order. However, this concentration of authority often compromises individual liberties and undermines the principles of democratic governance.
The lack of institutional capacity poses a significant challenge for states undergoing revolutions aimed at transforming the old autocratic structures. While revolutions can dismantle outdated institutions, they often fail to create stable and inclusive ones. This absence can lead to governance breakdown or a return to centralized control.
An American political sociologist, Barrington Moore Jr (1966), noted that economic pressures from significant changes can alienate supporters and strengthen counter-revolutionary forces. He illustrated this with Venezuela's Bolivarian Revolution under Hugo Chávez, which launched social reforms but collapsed due to economic mismanagement and overreliance on oil.
Additionally, external interference from groups supporting authoritarian governments can weaken revolutions through military action, sanctions, or backing counterrevolutionary movements.
Jack Goldstone, an American sociologist, political scientist, and historian, in his (2001) piece, critically analyzed revolution and rebellion in the early modern world. He argued that revolutionary governments encounter significant external opposition, which constrains their independence and chances of survival.
The Cuban Revolution endured largely due to Soviet support despite US efforts to undermine it, like the Bay of Pigs invasion and the embargo. Following revolutions often lead to revolutionary fatigue and disillusionment with ideals such as equality and justice, as ongoing instability wears on citizens. Hannah Arendt noted that the initial fervor often gives way to disappointment over unmet commitments.
The Iranian Revolution (1979), which began with anti-authoritarian goals, eventually resulted in a theocratic regime with authoritarian governance, raising questions about Iranians' collective perception of its outcome. Counter-revolutionary forces, such as displaced elites and military bodies, frequently resist and can reclaim power.
In the book Age of Extremes , the British historian Eric Hobsbawm (1994) argues that successful revolutions are uncommon because old ruling classes and their deep-rooted stakeholders, both domestically and externally, usually possess the means to hinder change. For instance, during the French Revolution, monarchist forces continually weakened the movement, leading to Napoleon's rise to power.
Why have numerous strong revolutions not been sustained in Bangladesh ?
Since the nation's liberation, examining post-revolution power struggles and authoritarianism is foundational to understanding the lack of a sustainable revolution in an independent Bangladesh.
After the 1971 Liberation War, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's leadership aimed to create a new state. However, internal divisions, economic issues, and political opposition led to a one-party rule (BAKSAL) in 1975, followed by substantial military rule until 1990.
Rounaq Jahan (2005) argued in her piece: "Bangladesh: Promise and Performance" that authoritarianism and elite conflicts hindered the establishment of democracy, resulting in coups and instability.
While military regimes framed themselves as stabilizers, their use of revolutionary rhetoric without implementing necessary reforms was unpopular among the state's citizens.
Fragile political institutions prioritize control over governance, leading to poor governance and disrupted citizen well-being. Strong institutions are essential for sustainable governance, but in Bangladesh, partisan politics, corruption, and patronage systems have consistently undermined this development.
Clear objectives allowed key movements in East Pakistan to gain recognition among the majority population. The Language Movement in 1952 aimed to establish “Bangla” as an official language, while the 1971 Liberation War sought self-determination against West Pakistani dominance. Badruddin Umar (2004) in “ The Emergence of Bangladesh ” identifies the Language Movement as a pivotal moment for Bengali nationalism, emphasizing the importance of cultural identity in fueling collective action.
Ahmed Rafiuddin's (2004) work, “ The Bengal Muslims, 1871–1906 ”, highlights how clear goals and national identity underpinned successful revolutionary movements in Bangladesh, leading to widespread support across social classes. In contrast to unsuccessful revolutions elsewhere, these movements involved students, workers, peasants, professionals, and civil servants.
Bose Sarmila (2011) in “ Dead Reckoning: Memories of the 1971 Bangladesh War ” describes the 1971 war as a social revolution, involving diverse participants across religions and classes, characterized by an inclusive and nationalistic spirit.
Effective leaders in revolutionary movements demonstrate significant charisma and actively engage with grassroots constituents, effectively aligning popular movements with specific political objectives.
This dynamic was exemplified by the Six-Point Movement of 1966 in East Pakistan, where nationalist leaders adeptly transformed cultural grievances into a coherent secessionist strategy. This approach channeled widespread public discontent into organized action, thereby mitigating potential chaos.
The oppressive policies enacted by West Pakistan, characterized by economic inequity and military repression, created a moral impetus for revolution. The violent crackdown known as Operation Searchlight in 1971 intensified calls for independence, fortifying internal solidarity while simultaneously garnering international support.
International backing proved critical to the success of the 1971 Bangladesh independence movement. It played a pivotal role in shaping military dynamics, securing diplomatic recognition, and amplifying humanitarian awareness.
While the primary driving force behind the movement was the local populace and the Mukti Bahini, external support was instrumental in facilitating the eventual liberation of Bangladesh.
In a parallel instance, the mass mobilization that occurred in 1990 culminated in the ousting of Hussain Muhammad Ershad’s military regime. This movement, propelled by extensive public engagement and international pressure, marked a significant transition from dictatorship to parliamentary democracy in Bangladesh.
The July-August movement in Bangladesh was underpinned by a sustained wave of mass protests against the autocratic regime that had been ongoing since 2009. This mobilization culminated in pivotal events on August 5, 2024, highlighting a significant coalition of support from both the elite and general populace.
This scenario illustrates a practical application of Lenin's theory on the necessity of mass participation and leadership to facilitate revolutionary change; the experience in Bangladesh demonstrates that without widespread engagement and strategic direction, achieving governmental control can prove exceptionally challenging.
Has the recent movement failed in Bangladesh?
To understand the challenges faced by movements in Bangladesh, it is essential to look beyond street demonstrations. While many mass movements gain momentum, they often struggle to effect lasting change due to structural, political, and social barriers.
Since Bangladesh's independence in 1971, efforts have been hampered by a lack of a unified ideology, societal fragmentation among political parties, internal divisions, weak institutions, economic disruptions, external opposition, and declining revolutionary ideals, all of which hinder the sustainability of post-revolutionary governance. Most importantly, movements or revolutions have failed due to:
(a) elites and vested interested groups’ manipulation in the process of transferring basic structural reforms within the state’s social, political and legal institutions;
(b) authoritarian reactions;
(c) internal divisions within the movement organizers and followers.
To achieve enduring change, movements require ongoing civic involvement, institutional partnerships, and a distinct vision for democracy, not merely the ousting of specific leaders or regimes.
Many movements are reactionary, focusing on removing leaders or achieving electoral victory without clear plans to reform institutions such as the judiciary or the police. These movements often lack institutional grounding, allowing the old system to revive once initial enthusiasm fades.
In Bangladesh, political parties frequently appropriate grassroots movements to enhance their electoral prospects, only to perpetuate corrupt practices once in office. This dynamic engenders a significant disconnect, wherein grassroots activists perceive themselves as marginalized, as political leaders exploit public discontent for their personal or factional agendas
In my assessment, drawing upon extensive longitudinal observations of Bangladeshi society, the pathway to sustainable transformation in Bangladesh necessitates a cultural revolution that fundamentally reconfigures societal values, norms, and institutional frameworks.
Unlike political revolutions that primarily alter governing bodies, cultural revolutions aim to modify the foundational societal constructs, thereby impacting domains such as education, the arts, and social interactions. The primary attributes of this transformative process include:
(a) Ideological shift to change national beliefs;
(b) Public mobilization for norm transformation;
(c) Repression of old values through censorship;
(d) State or movement-driven initiatives;
(e) Enduring effects on institutions like education and family.
Preserving the momentum and legacy of a mass movement is a complex but essential task. Following the July-August 2024 movement in Bangladesh, one of the most important challenges has been transforming public aspirations into sustainable democratic and institutional reforms.
Achieving this requires building citizens' confidence, strengthening public institutions, and fostering trust among domestic and international stakeholders. While significant opportunities have emerged, the long-term success of the movement will depend on the ability of political and social actors to work collaboratively toward inclusive governance and national development.
Bangladesh has the potential to improve its chances of sustaining a revolution or upsurge that truly changes society and governance by nurturing a cultural revolution. This would also create an atmosphere conducive to the flourishing of democratic ideals and a just society.
Dr ASM Anam Ullah (PhD) is an Australian senior academic, editor, human rights activist, political analyst, and OHS and industrial relations expert.

item.title: Reassess the economics of the Bay Terminal
item.description:
Bangladesh is aspiring to become a trillion-dollar economy, an export powerhouse, and a future regional manufacturing hub. Given these ambitions, investing in world-class ports sounds like an obvious step.
But successful nations are rarely defined by how much infrastructure they build. Instead, they are defined by the discipline they bring to the decision making around what to build, when to build it, and at what cost.
That is precisely why the Bay Terminal deserves a fresh, evidence-based reassessment.
If Bangladesh can unlock substantially more capacity from the ports it already has, shouldn't we wring out those gains before committing billions more to another mega-project while our purchasing power is already strained?
That question is no longer theoretical. In 2025, Chittagong Port Authority handled a record 3.409 million TEUs of containers -- including roughly 750,000 empty boxes -- while carrying 92% of Bangladesh's international trade and nearly 98% of its containerized cargo.
For an economy this size, a port carrying that much of the national trade load is not merely infrastructure. It is the country's economic heartbeat.
Yet beneath the headlines about new megaprojects sits a less-told story. Operational assessments suggest that simply modernizing what already exists -- the New Mooring Container Terminal, the Chittagong Container Terminal, the general cargo berths, and a fully utilized Patenga Container Terminal -- could lift annual handling capacity from roughly 34 lakh TEUs to about 46 lakh TEUs according to a study.
That is a nearly 35% increase without building a single new deep-sea terminal -- on its own, roughly equivalent to adding the throughput of a mid-sized port.
The picture becomes more compelling still. Matarbari Deep Sea Port is already under construction, and the completion of its first phase is projected to lift Bangladesh's total container handling capacity to approximately 54 lakh TEUs -- almost a 60% increase over current throughput. Add APM Terminals' new facility and Matarbari's second phase, and overall national capacity could reach around 88 lakh TEUs -- roughly 2.6 times what the country handles today.
These numbers invite an obvious policy question: Should Bangladesh first optimize, modernize, and fully use the capacity it already has -- and the capacity already nearing completion -- before committing to another capital-intensive port expansion?
This is not an argument against development. It is an argument for sequencing it well.
Singapore continuously modernizes its existing terminals while sequencing expansion decades in advance. The Port of Rotterdam invests as heavily in automation, hinterland connectivity, and logistics integration as it does in physical infrastructure.
Busan's competitive edge comes as much from operational productivity as from additional berths. In global port economics, capacity is one variable, productivity is the multiplier.
That distinction matters because of opportunity costs. Bangladesh remains a capital-constrained economy, and every additional billion dollars committed to one project is a billion dollars unavailable for energy security, rail connectivity, inland logistics, climate resilience, education, or healthcare.
Infrastructure planning, in that sense, is an exercise in capital allocation as much as engineering.
This is where the Bay Terminal deserves closer scrutiny. Accommodating larger, deep-draft vessels will require substantial capital dredging, along with recurring maintenance dredging over the life of the project.
One estimate places initial dredging costs at$150-160 million, with annual maintenance potentially reaching $20-25m -- though these figures need independent engineering validation.
For scale, the World Bank has already approved a $650m loan to help finance the breakwater and access-channel dredging alone, a reminder that headline dredging estimates for the project tend to be a floor rather than a ceiling.
These costs are not, by themselves, reasons to abandon the project. They are reasons to make sure every assumption behind it is rigorously tested.
Bangladesh has already learned this lesson once, at Payra. That port's experience shows how sediment dynamics, navigation constraints, and long-term dredging needs can significantly affect operational economics over time.
Bay Terminal is a different project with different engineering characteristics, and the two should not be treated as identical. But Payra is a reminder that a port's success is measured not by its ribbon-cutting ceremony, but by its ability to operate efficiently, sustainably, and economically over the following 30 years.
Encouragingly, reports indicate that the Bay Terminal feasibility assessment is being revisited. That should be welcomed. It is an opportunity to do something Bangladesh has rarely attempted: A comprehensive national port optimization strategy.
Rather than evaluating Bay Terminal in isolation, policy-makers should weigh it against every realistic alternative such as modernizing NCT and CCT, fully utilising Patenga, accelerating Matarbari, improving rail and inland container logistics, expanding automation, and widening private-sector participation.
Only then can the country work out which sequence of investments delivers the highest economic return per taka spent.
The debate, then, is not whether Bangladesh needs the Bay Terminal. It is whether the Bay Terminal should be the next investment or whether smarter, faster, and more cost-effective options can deliver the same economic benefits while preserving scarce public resources.
Nations rarely grow prosperous because they build the biggest infrastructure. They grow prosperous because they build the right infrastructure, at the right time, in the right sequence, with the discipline to question even their most ambitious ideas.
As Bangladesh charts its maritime future, that discipline may prove to be the most valuable investment decision of all.
Ashfaq Zaman is the founder of Dhaka Forum and a strategic international affairs expert.

item.title: The morning after: A question of accountability
item.description:
Bad things happen everywhere. That is the human condition, not a national indictment.
On the same day in late August that a family of four was killed in Bangladesh, a seventeen-year-old schoolgirl was stabbed to death in Sweden, and in Britain several young men died in a car crash during a police pursuit.
No society, however ordered, is spared sudden and terrible loss.
The measure of a state, then, is never whether tragedy occurs. It is what the state does the morning after.
In Sweden and in Britain, elected governments set the machinery of justice in motion -- investigation, disclosure, prosecution, public accounting. Bangladesh also has an elected government. Yet here the machinery too often produces an explanation faster than it produces evidence.
That is the difference that should concern every citizen. And minorities are simply where that difference becomes visible first.
Consider the case that prompts this. Ganapati Chakraborty spent his working life in a classroom. He taught at Rangpur Zilla School until his retirement last year, and by the accounts of his former students, he was the kind of teacher a town remembers.
On the night of August 20, in the Machuapara neighbourhood of Rangpur, he was killed in his own house, along with his wife Pritilata, their daughter, and their young son. The bodies were found two days later.
Two young men were arrested quickly and gave confessional statements before a magistrate. Since then, the police account of what happened inside that house has changed on more than one occasion, and the relatives of the dead have publicly disputed it.
On August 26, community organizations stood in a human chain before the National Press Club in Dhaka and asked for one thing: A judicial investigation, so that whatever the truth is, it may be established rather than announced.
Days later, in Chandpur, a businessman named Pintu Das disappeared together with his wife and their two sons. Relatives say he had been threatened. The police say they are looking into it.
Who killed the Chakraborty family is not known. What has become of the Das family is not known. Neither, at this moment, does the country -- and that is the point.
When the killing of a schoolteacher’s entire household produces an explanation faster than it produces evidence, something larger than one case is lost. What is lost is the public’s belief that the state is able to find out the truth at all.
What is happening is not sudden
It would be convenient to treat the Rangpur killings as an aberration, a crime like any other. The longer record makes that difficult.
Professor Abul Barkat of Dhaka University spent three decades studying what the Enemy Property Act and its successor, the Vested Property Act, did to this country’s Hindu citizens.
His finding was not about riots; it was about paperwork. Roughly 2.6 million acres were taken from Hindu families, and around 60% of Bangladesh’s Hindus were left landless.
In 2005 the United States State Department put the figure at about 2.5 million acres and estimated that nearly every Hindu family in the country had been touched by it.
The Vested Property Return Act was amended in 2011, largely because of the movement that Professor Barkat’s work helped to build. Restitution has still barely happened.
The census tells the second half of the story. In 1951, Hindus were a little over a fifth of the population. In 1974, 13.5%. In 2011, 8.54%. In 2022, 7.95%.
The absolute number has held roughly steady at 13 million, so this is not a community disappearing overnight. It is something slower and, in a way, sadder: A community that does not grow, because in every generation a portion of it quietly concludes there is no future here and leaves.
Professor Barkat gave this process a precise name. He called it unpeopling -- not the sudden violence that makes the newspapers, but the steady administrative and social pressure that makes staying unreasonable.
No government of Bangladesh invented this. Every government since 1971 has inherited it, and none has ended it. But it can only end under a government that decides to end it.
Beyond Minneapolis
Some years ago I wrote publicly, more than once, about the killing of George Floyd, as millions did who had never been to Minneapolis and had no personal stake in it.
I supported the movement that gathered under the words Black Lives Matter, and said so in letters to The New York Times. My sadness was such that I proposed, in one of them, that Washington Avenue be renamed George Floyd Avenue -- a small gesture of moral protest from very far away.
I want to be careful about why that case mattered, because the principle travels and the slogan is often misheard.
The principle behind those three words was never that only some lives matter. It was the opposite: That a life reliably ignored is the emergency -- that when a whole category of deaths dependably produces no consequence, the problem is not the individual death but the system around it.
The demand that followed was startlingly modest: Count the deaths honestly, investigate them as you would any other, and prosecute without regard to who the dead man was.
That principle has no borders and belongs to no one community. It can be applied in Bangladesh without importing a single foreign idea, because it is already written into our own constitution.
A country in which some citizens’ deaths are investigated seriously and others’ are explained away is not a country with a minority problem. It is a country with a rule-of-law problem -- and the minority is simply where that problem becomes visible first.
What should be done
The remedies are small, and each is within the government’s power.
Order a judicial investigation into the Rangpur killings, and let it go wherever the evidence goes. Find the Das family. Try these cases in open court, publish the verdicts, and accept the outcome even when it is inconvenient.
Instruct the police that a confession is where an investigation begins and not where it ends, and discipline officers who close files rather than solve them. Resume the return of vested property, which is 15 years overdue.
And let the state itself collect and publish honest national data on communal violence -- because at present the only figures available come from advocacy organizations, and a government that disputes those figures has an obvious remedy: Publish better ones.
Let me also say plainly what I am not saying, because in this country such things are heard before they are read.
I am not saying that the Muslims of Bangladesh are the enemies of the Hindus of Bangladesh. In every bad season we have had, including this one, it has been Muslim neighbours who sheltered Hindu families. I am not calling for retaliation of any kind; anyone who answers murder with murder has become the thing he feared.
And I am not inviting any foreign government to adopt this community as an instrument of its own quarrels. Minorities who become another country’s talking point end up less safe, not more. This is a Bangladeshi matter, to be settled in Bangladeshi courts.
Nor is this a Hindu matter alone. Impunity has no religion and no loyalty. The same police stations and the same courts that fail a Hindu family in Rangpur are failing Muslim families elsewhere, and the political killings that were promised to end have not ended.
Minorities are only where the failure shows itself first, because we have the least protection and the fewest voices raised on our behalf. We are the early warning. We are not the exception.
This is not, in the end, a plea for the protection of Hindus. It is a plea for the ordinary functioning of a state that means what it says.
Rajani K Saha writes from Sweden and is a practising physician.

item.title: Praxix Academy launches smart digital learning platform
item.description:
Praxix Academy, a next-generation digital learning platform, has officially launched in Bangladesh, aiming to make exam preparation more efficient, technology-driven and data-informed.
The platform combines digital learning materials, practice tools, artificial intelligence (AI), assessments and performance analytics to help students understand their strengths, weaknesses and overall level of preparation.
One of its key features is Praxix AI, a specialized AI-based tool designed to provide answers and explanations for Creative Questions (CQ) based on the National Curriculum and Textbook Board (NCTB) curriculum.
Praxix Academy offers an E-Library, Practice, Custom Exams, Praxix AI, Live Exams, Question Bank, Progress Reports, and Leaderboards.
The E-Library allows students to access syllabus-based materials through smartphones, highlight texts, add personal notes and use an on-screen AI tutor to understand difficult topics.
Its Practice feature uses the “Active Recall” method, allowing students to practise after studying a topic to reinforce learning and improve retention.
Students can also take customized, topic-based tests to assess their preparation, improve time management and reduce exam anxiety.
The Live Exam feature allows students from across the country to participate in examinations in real time and compare their performance with other participants.
The platform’s Question Bank includes previous years’ board examination questions, Cadet College tests and examination papers from leading schools, along with solutions.
Progress Reports use performance data to help students identify areas of strength and weakness and focus their study time accordingly. The Leaderboard allows users to track their position among students participating nationwide.
Praxix Academy Business Head Pronoy Mondal said students today have access to a wide range of educational content through YouTube and other digital platforms.
“However, access to content alone does not tell students how well prepared they are, how much they may score in an examination or where their actual weaknesses lie,” he said.
According to Mondal, the gap between learning and achieving the desired outcome can be addressed through effective practice, feedback and a clear understanding of one’s preparation.
“Praxix Academy has been developed as a practice-based learning platform. We want to track what students have learned, where they are making mistakes, which areas require more practice and how their preparation is progressing,” he said.
He added that the platform aims to support personalized learning by combining AI and modern technology, allowing students to practise according to their individual needs and capabilities.
Praxix Academy also plans to make conventional book-based learning more interactive through technology-enabled e-books, Mondal said.
The platform is currently offering early access.
Further information is available at https://praxix.academy.

item.title: Eight signs you're dating someone who's emotionally unavailable
item.description:
Relationship experts say emotional unavailability follows recognizable patterns, and identifying them early can prevent months of one-sided effort and confusion.
The signs are rarely dramatic. They show up as small, repeated moments — a conversation that changes direction the instant it gets personal, a silence where a real answer should be.
They will talk for hours about films, work, or daily life. But ask what they are actually feeling, and the answer shrinks to almost nothing — "I don't know," "I haven't thought about it," "I'm fine."
One instance is not a pattern. A closed door every time the conversation turns emotional is.
Early on, they are attentive — regular contact, warmth, compliments. But once the relationship starts to feel serious, something shifts. Contact drops off. The warmth cools.
For some people, growing closeness activates an old fear, and they respond by creating distance again. The pattern to watch is whether this push-and-pull repeats.
Say you tell them their distance hurt you. If the answer is consistently "you're overthinking this" or "you don't need to be this sensitive," that is worth pausing on.
Disagreeing with how someone feels is normal. Waving it away as baseless is not the same thing.
Every relationship has disagreements. But if a partner responds to conflict by shutting down, going quiet, or disappearing rather than working toward resolution, that becomes difficult to sustain.
Taking a moment to cool off during anger is healthy. Avoiding the issue altogether is not the same as taking space.
"Where is this going?" is a simple question. But if someone consistently deflects it, avoids a clear answer, or seems uncomfortable each time it comes up, it raises questions about their readiness for commitment.
Not everyone moves at the same pace, so patience matters — the real signal is whether that clarity ever arrives over time.
You share your fears, your past, your hopes. Their inner world, by contrast, stays a mystery. You know them; they do not let you in.
When one person consistently gives more emotionally than they receive, a quiet loneliness can build — even while the relationship looks fine from the outside.
A bad day, and you are the first call they make. A problem, and they come straight to you. But when your day goes badly and you need support back — they are suddenly busy, tired, or unreachable.
Healthy relationships run on reciprocity. Nobody can give equally every moment, but a pattern of one-sided giving eventually strains the relationship.
Sometimes a person enters a new relationship without having fully processed pain from a previous one. Betrayal, heartbreak, or prolonged emotional strain can make it hard to open up fully to someone new.
Carrying past pain does not automatically make someone emotionally unavailable. The real question is whether they are willing to work through it and make room for something new.
Experts caution against labeling someone based on one behavior alone. Some people are naturally quieter or more private. Others prefer to take relationships slowly. Work stress, family pressure, or emotional exhaustion can also cause temporary withdrawal.
What matters more is the pattern: Does the behavior repeat? Does the person try to communicate clearly? Do they take your feelings seriously? Are they making an effort too?
The reasons vary. Some grew up in environments where expressing feelings was discouraged. Others carry deep wounds from past relationships. Fear of rejection can also lead people to keep others at a distance — sometimes without fully realizing they are doing it.
Start by acknowledging your own feelings rather than dismissing them. If you repeatedly feel alone, uncertain, or neglected in a relationship, it is worth addressing directly — without blame.
Experts suggest a simple approach: "When you pull away instead of talking about something important, I feel alone and uncertain. I want us to have a space where we can both talk about our feelings."
Then watch the response. Does the person listen? Try to understand? Reflect on their own behavior? Or dismiss the concern again as "overreacting"?
Someone can be physically present every day, spend time with you, and care about you — and still be emotionally distant. Others say little, yet understand deeply, listen closely, and show up when it counts.

item.title: Six defining moments of Lionel Messi's Argentina career
item.description:
Lionel Messi announced his retirement from international football on Monday, six weeks on from Argentina's defeat in the World Cup final and after over 200 appearances for his country stretching across more than two decades.
AFP Sport looks back at the moments that defined Messi's career with his country.
- Inauspicious start -
Messi's international career began as a fresh-faced 18-year-old in 2005. His first cap was unforgettable for the wrong reasons -- ninety seconds after coming on as a substitute in a friendly with Hungary in Budapest, he was sent off for what the referee saw as an elbow.
The following June he made his first World Cup appearance in the 6-0 win over Serbia and Montenegro with which Argentina began the 2006 tournament in Germany.
Messi got his team's final goal in Gelsenkirchen -- the first game and goal of what would become a legendary relationship with the World Cup.
- First World Cup final -
Messi was 26 when Argentina headed to Brazil in 2014, but was already established as one of the greats thanks to his achievements with Barcelona.
There had been numerous disappointments with Argentina: quarter-final defeats, both to Germany, at the World Cup in 2006 and in 2010, the latter with Diego Maradona as coach. There was also a Copa America final loss to Brazil in 2007, and a miserable showing at the 2011 version of that competition on home soil.
Messi went to Brazil as captain of Alejandro Sabella's team, and made a flying start by scoring in every group game. The goals then dried up, but he took Argentina to their first World Cup final since the days of Maradona, only for the Albiceleste to fall short against Germany at the Maracana.
- 2016: His lowest ebb -
The 2014 heartache was followed by the misery of losing the following year's Copa America final on penalties to Chile. Messi therefore went to the 2016 Copa America Centenario in the United States on a mission to finally win a major international title. Argentina cruised to the final.
Chile stood before Argentina once again at the MetLife Stadium just outside New York, but the outcome was identical -- another defeat on penalties, with Messi this time missing his kick.
Messi, who had already won over 100 caps, was heartbroken.
"For me the national team is over," he declared. "I've done all I can, I've been in four finals and it hurts not to be a champion."
Six weeks later Messi changed his mind and agreed to come out of his brief international retirement.
- A winner at last -
The second half of Messi's international career could not have contrasted more starkly, with Lionel Scaloni's appointment as coach in 2018 proving a game-changer.
In 2021, in the middle of the Covid pandemic, Messi and Argentina went to Brazil for the Copa America and beat the hosts 1-0 in the final thanks to an Angel Di Maria goal to claim their first major title in 28 years.
- The crowning glory in Qatar -
Messi could, and perhaps should, have bowed out after the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, when the Barcelona legend -- by now 35 and playing for PSG -- found another level to drag Argentina to victory.
He scored seven goals and set up three more in seven games, including a brace in the epic final against France -- when he also converted his penalty in the shoot-out which gave Argentina the trophy for the third time in their history.
"Obviously I wanted to finish my career with this. I can't ask for any more," Messi said after that triumph.
But he wanted to play on a little longer as a world champion, and in the end he kept going all the way to this year's tournament.
- Another final defeat -
Messi skippered his country to another title at the 2024 Copa America before going into a record-equalling sixth World Cup this year in the USA. He was about to turn 39, but doubts about his age were blown away as Messi scored eight goals in his team's first five games and helped inspire them to another final.
Messi has played more World Cup matches than anyone else (34) and scored 21 goals overall. He became only the second player to appear in three different World Cup finals, but he and Argentina were abject as they lost in extra time to Spain -- an anti-climactic ending to an international career spanning 207 matches and 125 goals.

item.title: Tributes to 'eternal' Messi on Argentina retirement
item.description:
The football world on Monday paid homage to Argentine superstar Lionel Messi after his decision to retire from the national team.
Here are some of the main reactions to the announcement, which left fans and team-mates alike feeling bereft.
FORMER ARGENTINA TEAM-MATES Angel Di Maria, fellow 2022 world champion:
"It's so hard to read that we won't see you in the sky blue and white anymore. I only know that I was born in the right century to be able to see you, enjoy you, and on top of that, to share all these years with you on the national team."
Rodrigo De Paul, also a team-mate at Inter Miami:
"Just thank you, the greatest of all time, thank you for making us so, so happy, you can't imagine how many smiles you brought!! You are eternal."
Cristian Romero
"I love you, I admire you, and I will always be grateful for everything you gave for me and for our country. Eternal thanks, captain."
Argentine national team:
"Eternal thanks, Leo. We will love you until the end of our days."
OTHER REACTIONS Argentine President Javier Milei:
"Thank you so much, incredible man."
FIFA president Gianni Infantino:
"Congratulations @leomessi on an extraordinary international career which has inspired millions and redefined the beautiful game."
Antonela Roccuzzo, Messi's wife:
"What a privilege to have been by your side on this journey and to see you fulfill all your dreams. You deserved this story and so much more. We love you infinitely."

item.title: Dhaka ranks 11th among cities with worst air quality
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 11th among the world’s cities with the worst air quality on Tuesday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 105 at 10:08am.
According to the AQI scale, the city's air quality was classified as “Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups”, posing health risks to children, older adults, and people with heart or lung diseases, while the general public is mostly unaffected.
Kuching in Malaysia topped the global pollution list with an AQI of 579, followed by Dubai in the United Arab Emirates with 184 and Kinshasa in the Democratic Republic of Congo with 167.
An AQI reading of 101 to 150 is considered ‘unhealthy for sensitive groups’, while 151 to 200 is classified as ‘unhealthy’. A reading between 201 and 300 is considered ‘very unhealthy’, and anything above 301 is categorized as ‘hazardous’, posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides a daily indication of air quality by measuring the level of pollution and its potential impact on human health.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants — particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long faced serious air pollution problems, with air quality generally deteriorating during the winter months and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution contributes to around 7 million deaths worldwide every year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

Malaysia recruitment syndicate resurfaces with new tactics
item.description:
Bhaluka Overseas, which obtained a recruiting agency licence in 2022, has received approval to send 235 workers till 23 August. None of these workers are destined for Malaysia. However, the organisation is on the list of 25 agencies selected to send workers to Malaysia.

Md Abu Sohag Khan, the proprietor of Bhaluka Overseas, told Prothom Alo that he previously sent over a thousand workers to Malaysia under different agencies.

Similarly, he sent workers to Saudi Arabia. This time, he secured the opportunity to send workers directly and was automatically selected from Malaysia. He did not need to pay anyone for this.

Like Bhaluka Overseas, a total of 25 agencies have secured the opportunity to send workers to Malaysia this time around. Some members of the organisation of recruiting agency owners, BAIRA (Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies), stated that the names of previous agencies are not on the list this time. Unlike before, there are no direct names of ministers or parliament members' establishments.

However, the old masterminds behind the syndicates are now hiding behind unknown agencies. They have formed a new syndicate using different tactics, which may lead workers to spend Tk 600,000–700,000 to go to Malaysia.

A study by five organisations, including the US-based non-governmental development organisation Verité Incorporated, revealed that previously, each worker spent an average of Tk 544,000.

Prothom Alo collected data from the chosen 25 agencies for almost 23 years (from January 2004 to 23 August). Analysing these data from the Bangladesh Bureau of Manpower, Employment, and Training (BMET) shows that 17 of the 25 agencies have no experience in sending workers to Malaysia.

The remaining eight agencies collectively sent 1,612 workers. Of these, five agencies sent workers in numbers like 11, 74, 100, 150, and 202, while the other three sent 436, 333, and 306 workers respectively.

Malaysia has not specified any particular criteria while finalising the agencies. The opportunity has been seized by Bestinet, the owner of the Foreign Workers Centralised Management System (FWCMS) software Migrant, for Malaysian worker recruitment.

Aminul Islam bin Abdul Noor, a Bangladeshi-origin Malaysian citizen, also known as Amin Noor, owns it.

There are allegations that Amin Noor remotely controls the entire worker-sending business from Malaysia. Ruhul Amin alias Swapan, former secretary-general of BAIRA, acts as his representative in Bangladesh. Together, they have determined who will be in the syndicate. As before, they have also shared a portion of this with a group within the current government.

Swapan has been in hiding abroad following the fall of the Awami League in the mass uprising of 2024. His agency’s licence has been revoked, and he is facing a lawsuit with corruption investigations ongoing by the ACC.

Speaking about this, Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry State Minister, Md Nurul Haque, told Prothom Alo that the interim government sent a list of 423 agencies. From these, Malaysia selected 25 on their own. An additional 338 agencies have been given a chance to cooperate at the government’s request, making this a more positive step than before.

He further said that the ministry will set a limit to send workers at a lower cost. If any agency accused of trafficking or corruption is on the list, Malaysia will be informed, and their licences will be withdrawn.

Accused also on the list

There are 17 agencies, like Tania Trade, Satkhira International, A-Plus, Al Hayat Overseas, Valley Trade, Khan Jahan Ali Overseas, Bengal Human Resource, Earth Smart, Ath Taqwa, Motherland, Mangrove, Jewel Rinku Enterprise, Bangladesh One Overseas, Anwesha Air, Chandpur International, Godness Services, and Bhaluka Overseas, without any experience in sending workers to Malaysia.

The agency named The Anchor Care Global Migration and Consultant has received clearance for only 371 workers, with 11 going to Malaysia. Bangladesh One Overseas Limited has received total clearance for 795 workers, with no experience in sending any to Malaysia. These two agencies are on this year's list of 25 agencies.

United Gulf Services is on the list, owned by Laila Arjumand Banu. Previously, her husband Abdul Hai's company, Greenland Overseas, was in the syndicate. It is now run by their daughter, Rehana Arjumand Hai. Attempts to contact Laila Arjumand Banu were unsuccessful as she did not answer calls, nor did her daughter.

The ACC sent a letter to BMET on 23 July, asking for information on 57 agencies as part of a lawsuit claiming these agencies amassed illegal wealth through trafficking women abroad using forged documents in collusion with corrupt BMET officials.

Among these, three agencies—Godness Service Limited, General Trading Company, and Rifa International—are selected to send workers to Malaysia this time. Godness has no experience in sending workers to Malaysia, while the other two have sent some.

Despite several attempts, the owners of these three agencies did not answer calls. One person stated that they would inform the owner, but failed to respond further.

BAIRA members said that this time, the syndicate fee has to be 5,500 Malaysian ringgit (Tk 168,000). However, each visa must be purchased by securing a worker request for 8,000–9,000 ringgit (Tk 265,000–275,000). Thus, more than Tk 430,000 per worker will be siphoned off to Malaysia.

Malaysia selects the agencies

On 28 August, the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment in a statement said that agency verification and selection were done by a high-level joint committee formed with the Human Resources Ministry, Foreign Ministry, Home Ministry, anti-corrution commission, and law enforcement agencies in Malaysia. There is no involvement of the Bangladesh government.

According to the notification, an MoU was signed between Bangladesh and Malaysia on 18 December 2022, assigning the responsibility of selecting recruiting agencies solely to the Malaysian government. This reflects the submissive foreign policy of the Awami League government. The agreement expires on 31 December, making it challenging to alter terms in Bangladesh's favour, but the government has attempted to negotiate. The government hopes that the new MoU will protect Bangladesh's interests in agency approval.

Previously, during the Awami League government, it was also stated that Malaysia selected the agencies. Even after the market closure, a press conference by 100 agencies reiterated the same claim.

The interim government held multiple meetings with Malaysia to reopen the labour market. Malaysia set 10 conditions for listing agencies. Applications were received from agencies based on these conditions, initially qualifying 163 agencies. After deliberations, three conditions were relaxed initially, then another, resulting in a final list of 423 agencies sent to Malaysia by the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare.

Another strategy: Partner agencies

Workers are sent to Malaysia from 14 countries including Bangladesh. However, except for Bangladesh, no other country had such syndicate arrangements.

Although this time, 25 recruiting agencies each from Nepal and Bangladesh, and 10 each for India, Pakistan, and Myanmar have been approved. Yet, recruiting agency owners from these four countries have protested, demanding an open system providing equal opportunities for all instead of a syndicate-controlled limited agency privilege.

Sri Lanka and the Philippines were fully approved based on submitted lists. Nepal has initiated an investigation into the list of 25 agencies.

The Malaysia syndicate is a system where not all recruiting agencies are given the opportunity to send workers to Malaysia, but only a few. Initially, 25 agencies were part of the syndicate, later increasing to 100 in three phases.

There are accusations that large sums were taken from each agency to get their name on the syndicate list, and agencies in the syndicate collected at least Tk 150,000 as 'syndicate fees' per worker.

This allegation is currently under investigation by the ACC. Additionally, due to a lawsuit, 49 recruiting agency licences were revoked by the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment.

The Ministry states that the approved 25 recruiting agencies are among the 423 agency list formulated by the interim government. Malaysia's cabinet finalised 25 from this list, and following requests from the Bangladesh government, an additional 312 agencies are being allowed to send workers as 'Associate Recruiting Agencies.'

Recruiting agencies not on the list had previously sent workers to Malaysia. Four agency owners told Prothom Alo that their business of sending workers to Malaysia is long-standing. That is why they receive demands from companies there. They then contacted listed syndicate agencies, paying Tk 152,000 per worker as 'syndicate fees' last time. Associate agencies will work similarly. They cannot send workers directly or be identified by Malaysian employers as the approved agencies without experience.

Immediate-past senior vice president of BAIRA, Riazul Islam, told Prothom Alo that while a syndicate has been formed this time as well, a slightly new strategy is implemented.

According to him, if there were proper verification, unfamiliar agency names would not have been included in the list. This will increase worker expenses.

He further said that no applications were made for associate agencies; they were made associates without interest. Requests will not come directly to associates, but to the 25 agencies. In the past, over 817 agencies sent workers by paying fees. The number of associates has now reduced.

BAIRA members mention that 10 associates per main agency and 62 agencies under the government BOESL have been kept as associates for the current 25 main agencies. This is not a syndicate-free setup; it is merely a restructured presentation of the old system. During the past, nearly 1,400 agencies were listed with FWCMS, but starting with 10 in 2016 and 25 in 2022, it eventually approved 100.

Opportunity to send workers for free

The notice of the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry mentioned that following multiple ministerial meetings and discussions with Malaysian counterparts during Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s first foreign visit with Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar Raja, a vast potential for opening labour markets emerged.

According to the notice, following Bangladesh's special request, Malaysia agreed in principle to take 10,000 workers for free. The labour market will restart through the Ministry's BOESL by sending people to Malaysia.

In 2022, the government recruiting agency BOESL received demand orders to send over 10,000 workers to Malaysia but sent only about 1,500. Two responsible officials from BOESL said that workers were sent at no cost through BOESL, covered by the employer. That is there were obstacles from many. Consequently, more workers could not be sent, and BOESL incurred costs to obtain employment orders at the employer's expense.

The Expatriates' Welfare Ministry has urged caution against brokers and fraudulent syndicates to prevent the activities of intermediaries, stating that the process of sending workers to Malaysia is not finalised and is still in progress. The ministry will notify through a notice in due course and has warned against making any transactions beforehand.

Repeated syndicates, workers deceived

After being closed for nearly four years, when Malaysia's labour market opened in July 2022, Malaysia took over the responsibility of selecting recruiting agencies to send workers.

The Expatriates' Welfare Ministry sent a list of 1,520 recruiting agencies to them, and Malaysia made selections based on this list. Agencies of three MPs and an MP's family member during the Awami League era, along with Awami League leaders and City Corporation councilor’s agencies, entered the syndicate engaging in business.

They openly admitted having not sent any worker themselves, instead allowing other agencies to send workers in their name.

During the Awami League's 15 years, Malaysia's labour market was closed thrice. Each time, issues of syndicate formation for sending workers arose. Subsequently, allegations of irregularities, corruption, and bribery against the syndicate surfaced.

Malaysia's labour market first closed in 2009, reopened in late 2016, and closed again in September 2018 due to corruption and irregularities, reopening in August 2022 by forming a syndicate and closing back in June 2024.

Shariful Hasan, the Associate Director and Head of Migration Programme at BRAC, told Prothom Alo that the selection of 25 agencies proves that syndicates are stronger than the governments of both countries, leading to corruption, irregularities, and worker deception, not closing the recruitment system.

He further said that the recruitment continues through Amin Noor's system, signifying a significant failure of both governments. The agreement could have been amended, or new ones made, to send workers from the next year. Otherwise, reopening the labour market only for thousands of deceived workers does not make sense.

item.title: Nepal’s young PM faces gravest test after flood catastrophe
item.description:
TOPSHOT-NEPAL-DISASTER-FLOOD

Nepal’s rapper-turned-prime minister swept to power six months ago promising reform, but his young government now faces its gravest test after a glacial collapse unleashed catastrophe, analysts say.

A huge wave of freezing water and debris killed more than 1,000 people and left nearly 4,500 missing, with Kathmandu warning reconstruction costs could run into the “billions of dollars”.

The Himalayan nation has limited resources to confront destruction on such a scale, and the disaster is stark warning of the dangerous fragility of its mountain environment in a rapidly heating world.

But the August 26 disaster also came just ahead of the anniversary of last year’s September 8-9 youth-driven anti-corruption protests that toppled the previous government.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah, the 36-year-old former Kathmandu mayor widely known as “Balen”, won March elections on a wave of euphoria and promises of political change.

But he has since remained an elusive public figure—often seen in a sharp black suit and sunglasses, while largely communicating through social media.

He posted a message hours after the floods, urging the country to “stand together”, and has visited the disaster zones.

But, one week after Nepal’s deadliest disaster since the 2015 earthquake, Shah has still not publicly addressed the nation.

‘First major test’

Many say the scale of the catastrophe meant any government would have struggled with the rescue and relief effort.

“The government may be inexperienced, but it has done its best,” said Prakash Aryal, who has been searching morgues for his sister and her family, speaking to AFP at a Kathmandu hospital.

“The previous government would not even take calls, but this time there are officers everywhere helping people like us.”

Shah’s government said they were doing their best under the hardest of circumstances.

“Definitely, with this scale of disaster, often times there will be areas where we still need to improve,” Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told AFP in an interview.

“But we’re listening to people and if there are other challenges that we need to overcome... we’ll continuously ensure that we perform the best given the challenges.”

Shah was propelled to office with enormous support offering a new face of old generation of leaders.

“Expectations were exceptionally high when Balen came to office, especially among young voters who saw him as a break from Nepal’s political establishment,” said Brian Braun of the Control Risks consultancy.

“Six months in, the picture is more mixed.”

Braun said Shah could point to faster public services and an anti-corruption push, but voters were still waiting for the jobs, higher incomes and economic opportunities that formed a central part of his promise of transformation.

“The floods are now his first major test of whether that goodwill can survive a genuine crisis,” Braun said.

The crisis has also renewed scrutiny of Shah’s leadership style.

“He shies away from the cameras, he doesn’t address the nation at times and moments when people might expect him to,” said Ashish Pradhan of the International Crisis Group.

Yet Pradhan said there remained a widespread belief that Shah represented “a different form of politics”, particularly through his government’s emphasis on fighting corruption.

‘Optics are encouraging’

Kunda Dixit, publisher of the Nepali Times weekly, said the government’s early response had provided encouraging images of ministers and officials on the ground.

“During the earthquake, officials were hardly seen on the ground,” Dixit said, contrasting that 2015 response with the scenes from this disaster.

“Those optics are encouraging to the people but, in the end, the results have to be evaluated on how people are helped, and how efficient is the government in the relief and rescue operation,” he told AFP.

The disaster could also derail Shah’s ambitious reform agenda.

Pradhan said the scale of devastation meant reconstruction could take precedence over promises to transform the economy and accelerate development.

“Reconstruction might take the priority over reform,” he said, pointing to devastated hydropower projects, destroyed communities and the urgent need to restore livelihoods.

Braun warned the economic consequences could extend long beyond the immediate disaster, particularly because flooding damaged critical hydropower infrastructure in Nepal’s key electricity export sector.

The disaster also destroyed a key trade route with China and struck areas popular with trekkers and pilgrims, threatening further economic losses.

For Shah, analysts say, the catastrophe may also force climate change to the centre of Nepal’s national agenda.

Pradhan said Nepal may ultimately have to view climate change “as a national security imperative”, given the scale of destruction and loss of life.

Dixit, noting the millions of international aid being pledged for Nepal, said the government will be judged on how it is used.

“The real test will be how that money is spent—will it go first to the most needy people?” he said.

item.title: MoU signed for women’s football tournament
item.description:
With the dream of bringing grassroots women footballers onto a bigger stage, the first-ever Prothom Alo–Star News Women’s Football Tournament 2026 is set to take place this month.

Organised by Prothom Alo under the sponsorship of Star News, the tournament will feature 37 prospective women’s football academies registered with the Bangladesh Football Federation (BFF) as one-star academies and spread across the country. An MoU between Prothom Alo and Star News was signed yesterday.

At the MoU signing ceremony, held at Prothom Alo’s office in Karwan Bazar, Dhaka, General Manager and Head of Marketing Azwaj Khan and Star News CEO Mokhsedul Kamal Babu signed the agreement on behalf of their respective organisations.

Before the signing, Star News CEO Mokhsedul Kamal Babu spoke about various aspects of the tournament. “This is not just an MoU; it is a historic moment for women’s football in the country. This initiative will add a new dimension to women’s football,” he said.

He also said promising players would be selected from the tournament and given the opportunity to play for Nabil Group’s women’s football team, Rajshahi Stars FC. Operated by Nabil Group, Rajshahi Stars FC won the title in the most recent BFF Women’s Football League in its first-ever appearance. Nabil Group Head of Marketing Aktaruzzaman also spoke at the event.

At the event, Prothom Alo Managing Editor Anisul Hoque highlighted various initiatives taken by Prothom Alo to advance women’s football in the country. Expressing optimism about the tournament, he said, “This tournament will create a new platform for women footballers from remote parts of the country.”

Prothom Alo’s Chief Sports Editor also spoke about various aspects of the tournament. He said, “There has been tremendous response from women’s football academies across the country even before the tournament begins. Girls from different parts of the country will take part, which will help them rise to the highest level.”

Nabil Group Managing Director Aminul Islam attended the event and wished the tournament success. Expressing his commitment to taking the tournament forward, he said, “We want to take this initiative a long way. It is starting this year, and we want to continue the initiative in the future as well.”

Ahead of the tournament, a discussion meeting between the organising committee and representatives of the 37 BFF one-star women’s football academies was held on 22 August at Prothom Alo’s Karwan Bazar office. The participating representatives expressed their enthusiasm for the competition.

The preliminary round will be held across six regions on a knockout basis, followed by the final round in Dhaka. The champions will receive Tk 500,000, while the runners-up will receive Tk 300,000.

The primary objective of organising this tournament, which brings together women’s football academies from across the country for the first time, is to provide these academies with opportunities to compete. Such academies generally get few opportunities to play competitive matches. The tournament will therefore give their players a chance to showcase their talent.

Prothom Alo Editor Matiur Rahman, Associate Editor Sumana Sharmin, English Web Head of Content Ayesha Kabir, Head of Cultural Entertainment Kabir Bakul and Sports Department Special Correspondent Masud Alam, among others, were present at the event.

item.title: How much it costs to print banknotes
item.description:
The cost of printing Bangladesh’s banknotes has more than doubled since the Russia-Ukraine war began, as fuel and raw material prices increased. The rise in the dollar price also had a major impact on the increase in costs.

The lack of timely planning, emergency imports of raw materials by air and reliance on a single supplier have also increased the cost of printing banknotes, according to Bangladesh Bank sources.

Banknotes in Bangladesh are printed by the Security Printing Corporation (Bangladesh) Limited (SPCBL), which is a state-run entity that is operated by the central bank. Around Tk 4.5 billion is now spent annually on printing new banknotes.

An internal report of Bangladesh Bank shows that over the five years from fiscal 2020–21 to 2024–25, the cost of printing banknotes ranging from Tk 2 to Tk 1,000 increased significantly. For some denominations, production costs rose by more than 200 per cent. The costs have increased further since then.

Cost of printing each banknote

An analysis of the central bank report shows that printing costs increased the most for Tk 20 and Tk 50 notes over the past five years. In fiscal 2020–21, it cost Tk 1.58 to print a Tk 20 note, which rose to Tk 5.20 in 2024–25. This means the printing cost of the note increased by around 229 per cent.

Meanwhile, printing a Tk 50 note cost Tk 1.52 in fiscal 2020–21, which jumped to Tk 4.89 in 2024–25. During the period, the printing cost of the Tk 50 note increased by 222 per cent.

In fiscal 2020–21, it cost Tk 5.49 to print the highest-denomination Tk 1,000 note in the country. By 2024–25, the cost had nearly doubled to Tk 10.44. This means the cost of printing a Tk 1,000 note increased by around 90 per cent.

The printing cost of the widely used Tk 500 note in the country also increased significantly. While it cost Tk 3.74 to produce a Tk 500 note in fiscal 2020–21, the cost rose to Tk 6.58 in 2024–25, around 76 per cent higher than before.

For the Tk 100 note, the cost per piece increased from Tk 3.96 to Tk 5.58, representing a 41 per cent increase. The cost of printing a Tk 200 note rose from Tk 3.80 to Tk 5.21.

The production costs of lower-denomination notes have also been rising. In fiscal 2020–21, it cost Tk 1.20 to print a Tk 2 note, which rose to Tk 1.82 in 2024–25. The printing cost of a Tk 5 note increased from Tk 1.51 to Tk 2.33. However, the regulatory authority has stopped printing both denominations.

The cost of printing a Tk 10 note increased from Tk 1.42 in fiscal 2020–21 to Tk 1.57 in 2023–24.
